Within this framework, a `Riemann-Liouville-Heston' martingale model is defined which generalises these relationships to fractional counterparts. This model's implied volatilities are simulated, and exhibit features characteristic of leading volatility models.

papers.title: OPLoRA: Orthogonal Projection LoRA Prevents Catastrophic Forgetting during Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient fine-tuning of large language models but suffers from catastrophic forgetting when learned updates interfere with the dominant singular directions that encode essential pre-trained knowledge. We propose Orthogonal Projection LoRA (OPLoRA), a theoretically grounded approach that prevents this interference through double-sided orthogonal projections. By decomposing frozen weights via SVD, OPLoRA constrains LoRA updates to lie entirely within the orthogonal complement of the top-$k$ singular subspace using projections $P_L = I - U_k U_k^\top$ and $P_R = I - V_k V_k^\top$. We prove that this construction exactly preserves the top-$k$ singular triples, providing mathematical guarantees for knowledge retention. To quantify subspace interference, we introduce $\rho_k$, a metric measuring update alignment with dominant directions. Extensive experiments across commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation demonstrate that OPLoRA significantly reduces forgetting while maintaining competitive task-specific performance on LLaMA-2 7B and Qwen2.5 7B, establishing orthogonal projection as an effective mechanism for knowledge preservation in parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

papers.title: When is a polynomial in three variables cylindrical?
papers.abstract: We prove that a nonconstant polynomial $f\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,x_2,x_3]$ is cylindrical (that is, $f\in\mathbb{C}[x_1,x_2]$ after an invertible linear change of coordinates) if and only if its bordered Hessian determinant vanishes identically. The same conclusion holds over $\mathbb{R}$. We also give explicit counterexamples to this criterion in every dimension $n\ge4$.

papers.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
papers.abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. We discuss the root of the problem, which is intrinsic to the curved geometry rather than being a result of metric terms, coordinate system, or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

papers.title: Emulating DGEMM and ZGEMM with INT8 Matrix Engines on Intel Arc GPUs: Ozaki Scheme II on the Xe2 Architecture
papers.abstract: Double-precision matrix multiplication, real (DGEMM) and complex (ZGEMM), dominates the run time of dense linear algebra and electronic-structure codes. On affordable GPUs, however, FP64 throughput is a small and shrinking fraction of the throughput of the low-precision matrix engines. Ozaki scheme II closes this gap by reducing a floating-point matrix product to a handful of exact INT8 products followed by a Chinese-remainder reconstruction; the number of products sets the accuracy. We present what is, to our knowledge, the first implementation of Ozaki scheme II for Intel GPUs. Written in SYCL on top of oneMKL, it runs entirely on the device and exposes the full BLAS dgemm/zgemm interface. Making the scheme fast on the Xe2 (Battlemage) architecture required keeping FP64 arithmetic out of all memory-bound kernels, a branch-free residue computation, an FP32 evaluation of the CRT quotient with a proven safety margin, 16-bit limb arithmetic in the reconstruction, and work-arounds for performance cliffs of the vendor INT8 GEMM. On an Intel Arc Pro B60 (24 GB) the emulated DGEMM reaches 17.3, 12.1 and 9.3 TFLOP/s with $s=8$, 12 and 16 moduli at $N=8192$, and up to 21.1 TFLOP/s overall, i.e. 12-28x the native FP64 DGEMM of the same board. The emulated ZGEMM, which uses the 3M form exactly in integer arithmetic, reaches up to 27.4 TFLOP/s and is 13.7-17.8x faster than native ZGEMM for $N\ge4096$ at $s=16$. With $s\ge16$ the results are correctly rounded for well-scaled inputs and, using an extended-width residue path ($s=20$-24), also for inputs with wide exponent ranges, whereas native DGEMM rounds only 2-13% of the entries correctly. We also report worst-case accuracy, phase breakdowns, energy, an ablation study, a comparison with Ozaki scheme I, and a validated performance model.

papers.title: CorteXforge: Scenario-Based RF Dataset Generation on Real Testbeds
papers.authors: Andr\'ea Joly (CITI), Leonardo S Cardoso (CITI), Jean-Marie Gorce
papers.abstract: Deep learning for radio frequency (RF) signal analysis relies on large annotated datasets, yet synthetic datasets trade physical realism for controllability, while uncontrolled over-theair measurements offer realism but limited reproducibility. We present CorteXforge, a scenario-based framework for generating realistic and reproducible RF datasets on programmable software defined radio (SDR) testbeds. High-level RF scenarios are automatically translated into synchronized experiments executed on the SLICES-RI/CorteXlab platform, producing fully annotated Signal Metadata Format (SIGMF) datasets that capture hardware impairments and propagation effects. We validate CorteXforge through automatic modulation classification using ModForge, an over-the-air (OTA) dataset generated with the framework. Cross-domain experiments reveal a synthetic-to-real performance gap and show that synthetic pretraining remains beneficial for adaptation to OTA data. CorteXforge provides a practical foundation for reproducible RF dataset generation and future research on domain generalization.

papers.title: Robust Latent Variable Graphical Models: Exact Recovery and Fundamental Limits
papers.abstract: We study robust estimation of a Gaussian precision matrix that decomposes as a sparse matrix minus a symmetric, possibly indefinite, low-rank matrix, a structure that arises when latent-variable marginalization is combined with conditioning on linear measurements. The proposed convex estimator replaces the sample covariance by the centered Gaussian measure-transformed (MT) covariance, which preserves the signed graph of the sparse component under the nominal model, and penalizes the low-rank component by the nuclear norm of a congruence transform, an atomic norm that encodes structural side information. Our main result is a primal--dual witness theorem: under restricted invertibility and irrepresentability conditions on the Fisher information, the raw convex optimizer is unique, has no false edges, recovers the signs of all sufficiently strong edges, and has exactly the true rank and inertia. These conditions reduce to the graphical-lasso conditions when the low-rank part is absent, and we verify them from primitive incoherence and near-isotropy assumptions. Over a class on which they hold uniformly, we prove information-theoretic limits for Frobenius estimation, signed graph recovery, and inertia recovery. In particular, inertia recovery requires $N\gtrsim p/\nu_{\min}^2$ samples, where $\nu_{\min}$ is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue modulus of the low-rank part; the spectral beta-min condition of the witness theorem is necessary up to a $\sqrt{\log p}$ factor; and the Frobenius risk attains the minimax rate up to a factor $\sqrt{\mu(1+\min\{d,r\})\log p}$, where $\mu$ is the incoherence parameter, $d$ the maximal degree, and $r$ the rank. We further quantify robustness under Huber contamination, with a bias bound that is sharp for the MT functional and vanishes for remote outliers, and give a globally convergent linearized ADMM with closed-form updates.

papers.title: Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions for Logistic Classification on Manifolds
papers.authors: Guanhang Lei, Lei Shi, Xiaoming Yuan
papers.abstract: We study Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a connected compact smooth embedded manifold $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ without boundary and of intrinsic dimension $\varrho$. Two main challenges are to derive a fast oracle inequality without assuming a bounded Bayes function and to construct Gaussian approximants that exploit both the intrinsic dimension and the target's regularity without saturation. We address the first challenge through a Bernstein-type inequality whose constant depends linearly on the supremum norm of the predictor. Combined with localized complexity estimates, this yields an oracle inequality over separable normed function spaces. To address the second challenge, we establish a uniform Sobolev operator expansion and cancel its lower-order bias terms using a signed combination of Gaussian kernel integral operators at different bandwidths. Real interpolation then gives an $L_2(X)$ approximation error of order $\gamma^\alpha$ for functions in $B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$, where $\gamma$ is the bandwidth. By constructing the approximants directly on the manifold without ambient extension, we obtain a squared Gaussian RKHS norm bound of order $\gamma^{-\varrho}$. This construction thus overcomes second-order saturation while retaining norm control governed by the intrinsic dimension. When the marginal distribution has a density $g\in L_p(X)$, these results yield the logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n\bigr)^{4\alpha(1-1/p)/(4\alpha(1-1/p)+3\varrho)}$. We further show that clipping predictions yields the faster clipped logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n\bigr)^{2\alpha(1-1/p)/(2\alpha(1-1/p)+\varrho)}$. For bounded densities, its polynomial exponent matches that of the minimax optimal rate for squared-loss regression, and its corresponding excess misclassification risk also matches the minimax optimal rate.

papers.title: A Geometric Principle for Path Selection in Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: There are many types of path between nodes of a Directed acyclic graph (DAG), including the shortest and longest paths. Here, we ask whether the choice of path used in any analysis reflects the geometry of the latent space in which the DAG is embedded. To do this we define L_p-cube spacetimes, a family of continuous ordered spaces in which a single parameter p determines whether the ordered distance satisfies the ordered triangle identity when p>1, or the reverse ordered triangle identity when 0<p<1 or p<0, both of which are rarely studied. The forward connection kernel in the p<0 case has infinite hyper-volume, yet it is a well defined model. We then construct random geometric DAGs embedded in our L_p-cube spacetime and study their geometry. For p>1, where the ordered triangle identity holds, the shortest paths provide the closest approximation to the continuum ordered geodesic while for 0<p<1 and p<0, where the reverse ordered triangle identity holds, this role is instead taken by the longest weighted path. We also test the robustness of this relationship in a geometric citation model in which the random geometric DAG is supplemented by a preferential-attachment-type mechanism allowing connections beyond the strict geometric cut-off. The same broad correspondence between latent geometry and ordered geodesic path type is recovered. Our results show that the preference for shortest or longest paths in a DAG is closely connected to the geometry assumed for its latent space, and suggest that path structure can provide information about latent geometry, even when that geometry is not directly observed.

papers.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
papers.abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

papers.title: Flux Vacua, Asymptotic Periods, and Relatively Anosov Representations
papers.abstract:
We develop a topological method to detect classical flux vacua of M-theory on Calabi-Yau fourfolds with a single complex structure modulus using only asymptotic period data and monodromy information. To this end, we express the index of the F-term of the flux superpotential as a winding number along the boundary of the universal cover of the complex structure moduli space. The index evaluates to a sum over zeros and poles of a suitably normalized boundary F-term, where local contributions can be computed algebraically on a dense set of boundary points. Assuming a conjectured bound on the remaining contributions, sufficiently many sign changes of the boundary F-term guarantee a flux vacuum in the interior. We illustrate the method on the mirror Fermat sextic with explicit examples and a systematic flux scan.
  A main technical ingredient in our construction is a continuity result for projective period maps: we prove that the non-holomorphic (3,1)-period map extends continuously to the boundary of the covering space if the monodromy representation is relatively Anosov. In general, this property does not hold for holomorphic (4,0)-periods.

papers.title: Mapping AdS$_4$ quantum gravity via the Bethe Ansatz formula
papers.authors: Cheng Peng, Xuao Zhang, Ziruo Zhang
papers.abstract: The topologically twisted index of 3d ADHM theory can be written as a sum over solutions to the Bethe Ansatz Equations (BAEs) of the XXZ-type model constructed from quantum toroidal $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_1$. Via a novel numerical algorithm, we solve for all $p(N)$ physical solutions at $N\leq 21$, where $p(N)$ denotes the number of integer partitions of $N$. Surveying these solutions, we find that in addition to the known "1-cut" solution dual to dyonic black holes, where the gauge holonomies are distributed along a single curve in the complex plane, there are "dressed" 1-cut solutions dual to combined configurations of the black hole and M2-branes, $m$-cut solutions dual to $\mathbb{Z}_m$ orbifolds of the black hole, a discrete family of solutions interpolating between the 1-cut and 3-cut solutions, together with other exotic solutions, at each value of $N$. The free energy of the interpolating solutions cannot be matched with the on-shell action of any known bulk solution. The $1,2,3$-cut solutions and interpolating solutions all have a well-defined large $N$ limit, and their leading order distribution of gauge holonomies can be computed analytically. Whenever possible, we fit the contributions of the solutions to the index to all orders in the $1/N$ expansion with high-precision numerics, and extract the leading non-perturbative correction. With exceptions, these are matched with the results of equivariant localization in the bulk, and the action of wrapped M2-branes respectively.

papers.title: Short Point Lists for CNFs and Stronger Constant-Depth Circuit Hardness
papers.abstract:
We give a short-description decomposition of bounded-width CNFs. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every width-$b$ CNF on $m$ variables is an exact disjoint union of at most $2^{\varepsilon m}$ width-$b$ CNFs, each determined by $2^{O_\varepsilon(b)}\log(m+1)$ satisfying assignments.
  For every fixed $d\ge3$, we prove a worst-case size lower bound of $2^{\Omega_d((n\log n)^{1/(d-1)})}$ against depth-at-most-$d$ unbounded-fan-in AND/OR circuits with input negations for three polynomial-time Boolean families: inverse trace over binary fields, the Goldreich--Tal trilinear function, and OpenAI's polynomial evaluator with its original parameters. All parameter bits count as inputs. For inverse trace, every such circuit of size at most $S$, where $n\le S\le2^{c_dn^{1/(d-1)}}$, has uniform sign correlation at most $2^{-\eta_dn\log\log S/(\log S)^{d-1}}$. Here $c_d,\eta_d>0$ depend only on $d$. This improves on the classical parity correlation bound. The lower bounds combine the decomposition with restriction arguments; the correlation bound additionally uses common partial decision trees.
  We also construct exact nonuniform AND/OR circuits for inverse trace of size $2^{O(n^{2/3})}$ at depth eight and $2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}$ at depth nine. For every fixed integer $h\ge2$, the construction gives depth-$(4h+1)$ circuits of size $2^{O_h(n^{1/h}\log n)}$. The upper bounds implement finite-field evaluation and interpolation using circuits that enumerate intermediate states.

papers.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
papers.abstract: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(\beta, \delta)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^\beta, \beta \in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-\delta}),\delta \in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $\beta > 1, \delta>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $\beta\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $\beta > \delta + k(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $\beta > \delta + (k-1)(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.

papers.title: Exact spectral integrability of a finite-channel random Schr\"odinger operator: from fermionization of the Dyson--Riccati gas to Kontsevich integral
papers.authors: Yan V. Fyodorov, Pierre Le Doussal
papers.abstract: We solve exactly, for arbitrary finite channel number $N$, the Riccati dynamics of a quasi-one-dimensional random matrix Schr\"odinger operator with Hermitian white-noise potential in the $\beta=2$ unitary symmetry class. The associated Dyson--Riccati eigenvalue gas admits an exact free-fermion representation at any sample length $L$, which in the limit $L\to \infty$ expresses the density of states and the total Lyapunov growth rate exactly through a single Airy Hankel $\tau$-function providing multichannel generalization of $N=1$ Halperin--Thouless formulas. The $\tau-$function further admits an outgoing-contour Kontsevich matrix Airy integral representation. Its saddle-point and double-scaling analyses give, in a unified way, the finite-channel density Lifshitz tail, and the large-$N$ spectral edge. In particular, for $N\gg 1$ the sharp $N=\infty$ edge is softened within an $N^{-4/5}$ spectral window, with its profile governed by the tritronqu\'ee solution of Painlev\'e I. We conjecture universality of this quasi-one-dimensional scaling edge profile for a broad class of $\beta=2$ random band matrices.

papers.title: Quantum Fluctuations and Wigner Dynamics of a Carbon Nanotube Oscillator Driven by an Atomic Force Microscope
papers.abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes provide a useful platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion in regimes where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence can all influence the dynamics. We model the fundamental flexural mode of a carbon nanotube driven by an atomic force microscope as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator subject to a prescribed classical force and coupled linearly to a thermal environment. Starting from the generalized Langevin equation, we formulate the reduced dynamics directly in phase space, where the Wigner function evolves through a Gaussian propagator determined by dissipative linear transport, a deterministic force-induced displacement, and bath-induced fluctuations. For a Drude memory kernel, the retarded response is expressed through the three roots of a characteristic cubic equation. In the classical-noise limit, the three independent entries of the finite-time covariance matrix reduce to explicit finite sums over these response poles, eliminating numerical double-time covariance integration. We extend the construction to the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, obtaining a thermal frequency series representation that retains zero-point and low-temperature fluctuations. For an initial two-packet superposition, we examine interference attenuation and the integrated negative part of the Wigner function, which provides a phase space measure of nonclassicality. These results provide an explicit analytical framework for finite-memory quantum Brownian motion of bound oscillators and a tractable phase space description of driven carbon nanotube dynamics relevant to future quantum state preparation and quantum tomography experiments.

papers.title: Soft elasticity of soft shells
papers.authors: Andre M. Sonnet, Epifanio G. Virga
papers.abstract: Soft modes of a shell are one-parameter families of non-trivial deformations that preserve the elastic energy. We identify all soft modes of the soft shells described by the variational theory of put forward by Sonnet and Virga (2025). They are seen to be strictly connected with the Bonnet families, a special class of solutions to the problem posited by Bonnet, who asked whether there exist non-trivial isometries that preserve the mean curvature. Differential geometry deems as equivalent all surfaces in one and the same Bonnet family, but continuum mechanics is interested more specifically in soft deformation modes and the shapes they traverse, as they may describe ways to ignite fluctuations of soft shells that ideally require no energy to be activated. We give a general criterion for the existence of soft modes and a method to construct them based on a cascade of path integrations. We apply both criterion and method to some exemplary cases.

papers.title: Solving the Ho--Nguyen Conjecture for Gaussian Mixtures: Applications to Mixtures of Experts
papers.abstract: Over-fitted Gaussian mixtures can contain many parameter configurations with nearly the same density, making the order of density cancellation central to their parameter-learning rates. Ho and Nguyen encoded these cancellations in a polynomial system and conjectured its exact order as a function of cluster size. The key to resolving the conjecture is a common positive-variance shift that turns the coefficient equations into Gaussian moment matching. For every cluster size $\Mhn\ge2$, we prove that the real, nonzero-weight system has order $2\Mhn$: a sharp sign-change bound forces rigidity at that order, while positive Gauss--Hermite quadrature constructs a non-trivial solution through order $2\Mhn-1$. Population-density calculations at 110-digit working precision recover the predicted leading term for two to six components; finite multistart searches recover the same observed powers for two to five components, with smaller finite-scale constants for three to five components. For parameter learning, the exact order gives an explicit pointwise maximum-likelihood exponent and an exact local minimax order on specified shrinking neighbourhoods of a fixed known mixing measure. The same coefficient viewpoint separates high-order cancellation from exact parameter symmetries in mixtures of experts. Synchronized replication preserves the conditional density while keeping the corresponding parameter losses positive in two broad standard-softmax classes, showing why statistical rate arguments must account for exact parameter symmetries.

papers.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
papers.abstract: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this shows for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we establish an exponential iteration lower bound for termination of a Dantzig counterpart with unrestricted costs and prove that it admits a strongly polynomial implementation with unit weights.

papers.title: Pfaffian solutions to the Ernst equation
papers.abstract: We show that the Yamazaki-Hori solution to the Ernst equation can be represented in the Pfaffian form. We also discuss the consequences of this result for Nakamura's conjecture on the relation between the Ernst equation and the 2D Toda model.

papers.title: Beyond exponential tilting: sharp asymptotics and improved importance sampling for rare events
papers.authors: Mingxin Li, Hans Reimann, Timo Schorlepp, Georg Stadler
papers.abstract: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. While this tilt is log-efficient, we show that the coefficient of variation of the resulting estimator still grows like $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$ in the small-noise limit $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Motivated by sharp large deviation asymptotics and the local geometry of the event set at the minimizer, we propose improvements using a control variate or an anisotropic, non-Gaussian proposal. We prove, up to truncations that hold with high probability, and confirm empirically in high-dimensional examples, that the former bounds the coefficient of variation and the latter makes it vanish, so that a bounded number of samples suffices. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg--de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.

papers.title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events
papers.authors: Qinyi Wang, Anya Katsevich, Shanyin Tong
papers.abstract: We propose GeoIS, a new importance sampling method for estimating rare event probabilities for an underlying Gaussian distribution that exploits asymptotic theory and local event geometry. The proposal distribution is a mixture of two components. The first component draws a Gaussian along the boundary near the instanton and adds to it an exponentially distributed shift into the rare event. This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy's performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.

papers.title: Theoretical Foundations of Sequential Dynamic Programming
papers.abstract: Many economic problems have several controls per period, whose joint choice is subject to the curse of dimensionality. Solving them in stages is computationally cheaper, but no general result says when staging is exact. I develop a separability theory, discrete choices and non-concave objectives included: staging is exact if utility, transitions, and constraints depend on earlier decisions only through a state passed forward. For each ordering the smallest such state exists and is unique up to relabeling. Any state that keeps staging exact for all preferences over later decisions and the future must carry everything the smallest one carries for the transition. For affine primitives, the smallest state consists of the linear combinations, such as cash-on-hand, on which later outcomes depend. Its dimensions pick the order whose largest stage is smallest. In a six-choice household model, each stage chooses one variable on a three-dimensional state, the joint problem all six.

papers.title: Data-Driven Minimum Energy Control for Stochastic Linear Systems with Finite Sample Guarantees
papers.abstract: The open-loop minimum-energy control (MEC) problem asks for control inputs that minimize the control energy while ensuring the terminal state reaches a desired value. In this paper, we study the open-loop MEC problem for stochastic linear time-invariant systems. We consider a variety of stochastic constraints that enforce the terminal error to be \emph{small}, and show that Stochastic MEC (SMEC) problem can be formulated as a QCQP. We obtain the optimal solution for SMEC and show that it generalizes the well-known Deterministic MEC problem by introducing novel stochastic variants of controllability and Gramian matrices and show that there exists a fundamental lower bound on the optimal control energy which cannot be overcome by increasing the time horizon of the problem. We then extend the formulation to systems with unknown dynamics using maximum-likelihood estimation and conformal calibration, and compare these approaches with direct sample-based estimation that do not incorporate structural information of SMEC problem into account. Further, with the help of bias-variance analysis, we show when incorporating structural information proves to be better than direct sample based approach. Finally, we establish finite-sample high-probability upper bounds on optimal-cost sub-optimality and original constraint-violation probability under the data-driven controller, quantifying their dependence on the number of experiments, number of samples per experiment, system dimension, input sequence dimension, and noise-to-signal ratio. Using simulations, we validate the theoretical results numerically.

papers.title: Big Secrets Small Shares: Revisiting Secure Multi-Party Computation
papers.authors: Wilton Kim, Van Long Phuoc Pham, Stanislav Kruglik, Han Mao Kiah
papers.abstract: At CRYPTO 2007, Damg{\aa}rd and Nielsen introduced a preprocessing approach to multi-party computation (MPC) to achieve linear communication complexity. Another approach to reduce communication complexity was proposed by Cramer, Damg{\aa}rd, and de Haan at EUROCRYPT 2007, which involved using ramp-secret sharing schemes to jointly share base-field components of secrets from the extension field. In this paper, we combine these two ideas to achieve a non-asymptotic reduction of communication cost in a multi-phase MPC setup. We introduce a new modification of the ramp secret sharing scheme, called compact sharing, and tailor the MPC protocol to accommodate this modification. Compact sharing masks the polynomial coefficients that would otherwise leak during degree reduction. The protocol provides perfect security against static semi-honest adversaries under an explicit tradeoff between the corruption threshold and the extension degree. When the extension degree scales linearly with the number of parties, the gate-evaluation core achieves constant communication overhead relative to an extension-field element, amortized over full preprocessing batches; input and output communication is counted separately.

papers.title: Minimum-Time Escape from the Conic Field of View of a Reeds-Shepp Pursuer: Classification and Game Value for a Slower or Equally Fast Evader
papers.abstract:
We study minimum-time escape of an omnidirectional evader from the forward conic field of view of a Reeds-Shepp pursuer with minimum turning radius $r$. For speed ratio $
u$ and cone half-angle $0<\alpha<\pi/2$, we prove a global escape/holding classification: straight reversal holds the whole cone for $
u\le\sin\alpha$, escape is confined to a barrier-bounded dart for $\sin\alpha<
u\le1$, and escape is possible from every state for $
u>1$. For the slower or equally fast evader, $\sin\alpha<
u\le1$, we construct the solution with Isaacs' characteristics and verify it in feedback form, using a Filippov pursuer relay and a one-sided evader branch. The finite escape time is the first root of one scalar equation, and the holding region is bounded by the nonusable parts of the rays and a barrier that closes with a convex corner on the front axis. Sample-and-hold counter-controls show that this escape time is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except the corner. There the two strategy values differ: the pursuer's is infinite, whereas an evader that chooses which barrier branch to cross from the initial germ of the pursuer's control escapes before the barrier time $	au_I$, which is the evader's exact strategy value. An independent level-set solver, refined on fixed comparison points, agrees with the closed-form escape time and reproduces the holding region at the tested parameters.

papers.title: Learning the open string spectrum with neural networks
papers.abstract: The tree-level open superstring has an integer mass-squared spectrum on linear Regge trajectories. To what extent is this fixed by consistency conditions: locality, analyticity, crossing, unitarity together with the requirement that $2\to2$ scattering minimize the entanglement it generates? Using the local two-channel crossing symmetric dispersion relation with one-parameter ambiguity ($\lambda$-CSDR) we set up a bootstrap treating both the mass-squared spectrum and the partial-wave coefficients as unknowns which lets the machine learning algorithm to learn the mass-squared spectrum and partial-wave coefficients simultaneously, going beyond earlier work in which the spectrum was fixed. Using the local three-channel crossing symmetric dispersion relation with one-parameter ambiguity we obtain, within the class of amplitudes with soft Regge behavior and infinite higher-spin tower, a bound on the leading Wilson coefficients that we compare with existing bounds and trace to spin-0 dominance. We locate the Virasoro-Shapiro amplitude in the allowed region of the Wilson coefficients space. For amplitudes with two-channel crossing symmetry we find that a Non-dual amplitude exhibits a Polchinski-Strassler type transition from Regge to power-law behavior.

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
papers.authors: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
papers.abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.

papers.title: Constant Step Sizes for Muon-Type Spectral Optimizers on Strongly Convex Quadratics
papers.authors: Pratik Jawanpuria, Bhabatosh Garai, Bamdev Mishra
papers.abstract: Muon and related optimizers update a weight matrix with a spectrally transformed gradient. In this work, we study such spectral optimizers with a constant step size on strongly convex matrix quadratics, which isolate the effect of the update from the confounds of nonconvexity, noise, and step size schedules. We analyze an update using two quantities: the gain, which is the factor by which it amplifies the gradient along each singular direction, and the length, which is the norm of the update. These two quantities place the popular spectral updates in three regimes with different behavior: (i) with a bounded gain, the iterates behave like preconditioned gradient descent and converge for step sizes set by the largest curvature; (ii) with an unbounded gain but a vanishing length, they still converge, with the admissible step sizes set by the total curvature instead; and (iii) with a non-vanishing length, they do not converge for almost every initialization. Interestingly, the practical variants of Muon fall in all three regimes, depending only on how the update is normalized and scaled and not on the polynomial that approximates the polar factor. Experiments validate these findings.

papers.title: 5D Runge-Lenz Vector from Symplectic Reduction of 8D Harmonic Oscillator
papers.authors: Hitoshi Ikemori, Shinsaku Kitakado, Yoshimitsu Matsui, Toshiyuki Okubo, Toshiro Sato
papers.abstract: We derive the Runge-Lenz vector of the five-dimensional Kepler problem from the eight-dimensional harmonic oscillator through symplectic reduction. By rewriting the moment maps of the harmonic oscillator in terms of five-dimensional gamma matrices and the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ generators associated with the symplectic reduction, we identify the moment map expected to yield the Runge-Lenz vector. We then perform the reduction with respect to the SU(2) symmetry, derive the five-dimensional Kepler Hamiltonian, and show explicitly that the identified moment map reduces to the Runge-Lenz vector.

papers.title: Free-field realizations of $\mathcal{N} = 1$ supersymmetric $\mathcal{W}$-algebras associated with Lie superalgebras $B (n - 1 , n)$ and $B (n , n)$
papers.abstract: We extend the recursive construction of free-field realizations proposed by Ide, Ito, and Miyazaki to the $\mathcal{N} = 1$ supersymmetric $\mathcal{W}$-algebras $\mathcal{SW} B (n - 1 , n)$ and $\mathcal{SW} B (n , n)$, associated with the Lie superalgebras $B (n - 1 , n)$ and $B (n , n)$, respectively. We obtain explicit free-field realizations of $\mathcal{SW} B (0 , 1)$, $\mathcal{SW} B (1 , 1)$, $\mathcal{SW} B (1 , 2)$, and $\mathcal{SW} B (2 , 2)$. In particular, the realizations of $\mathcal{SW} B (1 , 2)$ and $\mathcal{SW} B (2 , 2)$ are new. Using these realizations, we compute central charges, conformal weights, and eigenvalues of the generating currents on free-field highest-weight states, and construct the local integrals of motion $I_1$, $I_3$, and $I_5$.

papers.title: Computing excited states of dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates by constrained gentlest ascent dynamics
papers.authors: Fu Zheng, Wei Liu, Xu Qian
papers.abstract: Dipolar Bose--Einstein condensates (BECs), i.e., BECs with long-range dipole-dipole interactions (DDI), exhibit extraordinarily rich physics and serve as a versatile experimental platform for exploring exotic quantum states of matter. Within the mean-field framework, a dipolar BEC can be described by the Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) model with a DDI term. Its stationary states consist of the ground state, which minimizes the GP energy functional under the normalization constraint, and excited states, which are higher-energy critical points that typically correspond to constrained saddle points. Excited states encode collective excitation modes and play a key role in the dynamical stability and quantum phase transitions of cold-atom systems. However, in contrast to the extensively studied ground state, they remain far less explored numerically, especially in dipolar systems. In this work, we develop a numerical method based on the constrained gentlest ascent dynamics (CGAD) that systematically computes excited states of dipolar BECs by stably targeting constrained saddle points with any prescribed Morse index. Specifically, a semi-implicit sine-pseudospectral discretization with an orthonormalization correction step is adopted, and the nonlocal DDI terms are evaluated efficiently and accurately via the nonuniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT). The resulting scheme is applied to one-, two-, and three-dimensional dipolar BECs, enabling a detailed numerical investigation of their excited states. Remarkably, our simulations reveal that excited states can persist even in regimes where the ground state of the condensate becomes mean-field unstable. This work provides a computational framework for studying excited states in dipolar quantum gases and offers insights for future theoretical and experimental investigations.

papers.title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
papers.authors: Pietro Carlo Boldini, Yifu Chen, Marios Kotsonis
papers.abstract: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.

papers.title: The Fer expansion of a driven spin under $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ operations cannot terminate beyond first order
papers.authors: Lorenzo Bagnasacco, Daniel Burgarth, Vittorio Giovannetti, Kazuya Yuasa
papers.abstract: The Fer expansion writes the propagator of a driven quantum system as an ordered product of exponentials, each generated by the time integral of an effective Hamiltonian that governs the evolution left over by the previous factors. It can be stopped after finitely many factors whenever this leftover evolution is known in closed form, for instance when the effective Hamiltonian commutes with itself at all times, or precesses about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, in any representation, from a qubit to a spin of any size, we resum the Fer recursion into a closed map on curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We prove that, for a real-analytic drive, in both cases the expansion stops beyond the first factor only trivially, when the first exponential is already exact.

papers.title: Annealed correlation and quenched noise sensitivity in biased deep neural networks
papers.abstract: In earlier work by Jonasson, Steif and Zetterqvist (2023), fully connected deep neural networks with layers of width $n$, i.i.d.\ standard Gaussian weights, sign activations and no bias terms were shown to be annealed and quenched noise sensitive with respect to any joint probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}$ on the input $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ and its perturbation $\boldsymbol{\eta}$ satisfying a mild positive-correlation condition and $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbol{\eta} \in \{\boldsymbol{\omega},-\boldsymbol{\omega}\}) \to 0$. Here we add independent Gaussian biases of the natural order and show that quenched noise sensitivity is retained over a broad range of depths, indeed under the slightly weaker assumption that $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{\eta}) \to 0$. Thus, subject to the positive-correlation condition, quenched noise sensitivity holds under the minimal requirement that the perturbed input is asymptotically unlikely to coincide with the original input. At the same time, the annealed covariance remains bounded away from zero and is entirely accounted for by fluctuations in the network-dependent output means.

papers.title: When Momentum Helps Polyak--Ruppert Averaging
papers.authors: Alexandra Suvroikova, Darina Dvinskikh, Yuriy Dorn, Alexander Gasnikov
papers.abstract: Polyak--Ruppert averaging gives SGD and momentum methods the same asymptotic covariance. We characterize how fast finite runs reach it and how far they can be parallelized. For strongly convex quadratics with additive noise, we prove an online--offline bridge: the empirical risk minimizer on the samples of a tail average is one Newton step from the tail-averaged query point of any online procedure. For SGD, heavy ball, and Nesterov's method with constant momentum, this step is a boundary term at the two ends of the tail and splits the gap to the offline estimator into center, covariance, and shape errors. Necessary and sufficient conditions show that, on the least curved direction, the center error sets the pace: SGD needs $m\gg\kappa^2$ rounds but momentum only $m\gg\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number, so at sample size $N$ the critical batch size grows from $\Theta(\sqrt{N}/\kappa)$ to $\Theta(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$. The covariance error separates the momentum methods: heavy ball has relative variance excess $\Theta(\kappa^{3/2}/m)$ along the stiffest direction, whereas Nesterov has relative error $O(\sqrt{\kappa}/m)$ in every direction. The shape error is method-independent by a Berry--Esseen bound uniform in $\kappa$ and batch size, so confidence intervals are valid when the other two errors vanish. We further examine how the conclusions change under heavy-tailed or state-dependent noise and clipping, and establish a first-order comparison with ERM for nonlinear Nesterov averaging under explicit conditions.

papers.title: The ABC-equation revisited: missed (quasi) integrable cases. Part II: extensions and actions
papers.abstract:
We continue here the study of the \textsc{ABC}-equation
  $Au_xu_{yt} + Bu_yu_{xt} + Cu_tu_{xy} = 0$, $A$, $B$, $C\in\mathbb{R}$ and
  using the results obtained in the first part construct new quasi-integrable
  structures and compute their actions on symmetries and cosymmetries.

papers.title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning and Inference via Measure-Indexed Kernel Ridge Regression
papers.authors: Zuofeng Shang, Tianyang Hu, Fan Yang, Yingcong Li
papers.abstract: In-Context learning enables an estimator, trained across multiple tasks, to adapt to a new unseen task solely through its in-context samples, without any parameter refitting. Despite growing interest in the statistical foundations of in-context learning, two gaps still remain. First, existing convergence results do not characterize the distributional behavior of the in-context learning estimators. Second, classical nonparametric methods are not designed to handle the measure-valued inputs that in-context learning naturally produces. We address both gaps by developing a measure-indexed reproducing kernel Hilbert space framework, in which the adaptivity of the estimator is captured through the dependence of a mean functional on the empirical measure of the context. Within this framework, we propose a measure-indexed kernel ridge regression estimator computed from multiple independent tasks and establish its minimax-optimal convergence rate. We further prove that the proposed estimator is pointwise asymptotically normal, enabling the construction of confidence intervals for the mean and prediction intervals for the response on an unseen task. Notably, the estimator achieves valid uncertainty quantification without any refitting when adapting to a new task. As a special case, our framework recovers classical distributed nonparametric regression when all tasks share the same underlying function. The proposed framework is illustrated through a latent Gaussian process example.

papers.title: Surface defects on lens space and transfer matrices
papers.authors: Kazunobu Maruyoshi, Toshihiro Ota, Masahito Yamazaki
papers.abstract: We study surface defects in four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories of class $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{N}=1$ theories of class $\mathcal{S}_k$ placed on $L(r,1)\times S^1$. The lens space index depends on the fugacities $p$ and $q$, and the effect of the defects on it is captured by difference operators acting on the fugacities and holonomies of flavor symmetries. For theories of type $A_1$ we determine in closed form the difference operators for the basic defects, labeled by $p^r$, $q^r$ and $pq$, and show that for odd $r$ there exist additional elementary defects, whose operators shift the holonomy by one half modulo $r$. All the operators commute, and the elementary operators generate the others. For even $r$ the same holds once the holonomy is extended to a twisted sector. We show that the elementary operators are traces of $L$-operators whose entries generate a Sklyanin algebra, with nome $q^r$ and shift $pq$. The lens space enters only through the parameters of the algebra and through its representation, which is realized on a doubled holonomy label. The $p$- and $q$-type algebras form a lens space version of the elliptic modular double. For class $\mathcal{S}_k$ theories we propose, and test in several ways, that the defect operators are transfer matrices of inhomogeneous spin chains built from these $L$-operators. Throughout, we use the TQFT structure of the lens space index, which follows from S-duality, both to fix and to check the operators.

papers.title: From Market Signals to Maintenance Decisions: Grid-Informed Maintenance Optimization in Offshore Wind Farms
papers.authors: Keyi Wang, Robert Mieth, Ahmed Aziz Ezzat
papers.abstract: The reliable and cost-effective integration of large-scale offshore wind farms into power systems is largely influenced by maintenance operations. To date, power producers primarily rely on farm-level information (e.g., health signals, power generation, weather conditions) for maintenance planning of wind turbine fleets. We propose to consider additional grid-level information in maintenance operations, such as generation curtailment and market pricing. Periods of high generation curtailment or negative electricity pricing can be viewed as opportunities for preventive maintenance, since assets are fully or partially shut down due to grid-imposed constraints. We first analytically establish that access to market information has non-negative economic value for maintenance scheduling under a stylized setting, providing a theoretical foundation for treating market and grid information as a maintenance opportunity. We then formulate a grid-informed opportunistic maintenance scheduling model as a receding-horizon mixed integer linear program that jointly leverages both farm- and grid-level signals under realistic conditions to determine a maintenance plan for offshore wind turbines. Considering a 600-MW offshore wind farm in the United States, our proposed method reduces annual maintenance costs by up to 10%, while enhancing asset availability and resource utilization, relative to advanced maintenance models that solely rely on farm-level information.

papers.title: Painlev\'e II connection problem revisited
papers.authors: Nikolai Iorgov, Oleg Lisovyy, Noam Tamarin, Yurii Zhuravlov
papers.abstract: We study the inhomogeneous Painlev\'e II equation for generic monodromy data. Using Kapaev's asymptotic formulas, the parameters of Zak transform representations of the Painlev\'e II tau function on six special rays $\arg t=\frac{\pi p}{3}$ ($p=0,\ldots,5$) in the complex time plane are expressed in terms of Stokes parameters of the associated linear system. We then solve the connection problem for the tau function between these special rays, and provide analytical and numerical checks of our result.

papers.title: A twisted Marchenko lemma and applications
papers.authors: Jun-Yang Zhang, Shi-Hao Li, Shou-Feng Shen
papers.abstract: We develop a twisted Marchenko lemma with applications into non-commutative two-component integrable systems. Starting from a twisted differential equation, we introduce the corresponding two-component Wronski matrix $W_{n,m}(\boldsymbol\phi,\boldsymbol\psi)$. Under the Marchenko lemma conditions, the logarithmic derivative $(\partial W_{n,m})W_{n,m}^{-1}$ satisfies nonlinear equations, whose two-component projections yield a non-commutative two-component KP equation, while a single-component reduction recovers the non-commutative Burgers equation, KP equation and DS equation. A direct approach based on two-component quasi-Wronskians is developed, from which a higher-order non-commutative two-component KP equation is generated with matrix-valued solutions. Reductions of the seed functions of the non-commutative two-component KP hierarchy yield the one-component counterpart, while a stepwise reduction of those for the two-component KP equation gives the non-commutative DS and NLS equations.

papers.title: Likelihood-Based Confidence Curves for Bounded Parameters
papers.authors: Hedvig Borgen Reiersrud, Clara Bertinelli Salucci, Riccardo De Bin, Alessandra Rosalba Brazzale
papers.abstract: When a parameter is bounded, the likelihood ratio statistic does not generally follow the chi-square limit distribution of Wilks' theorem. In fact, its asymptotic null distribution depends on the distance from the null value to the boundary, interpolating between the chi-bar-square law on the boundary and the chi-square law in the deep interior of the parameter space. We derive this distribution and use it to construct confidence curves, which are nested collections of two-sided confidence intervals or regions, for bounded parameters. We extend the existing result for the scalar parameter to a two-dimensional parameter with one or both components bounded. As the bivariate distributions are integrals of normal distributions, which are not reducible to standard statistical functions, we also give a simpler approximated distribution obtained by moment-matching. We illustrate the methods on a canonical analysis from high-energy physics, namely the Poisson signal-plus-background experiment.

papers.title: Timing and Reliability Limits of Position-Assisted UWB Multicast Audio
papers.abstract: One-to-many ultra-wideband (UWB) transport can disseminate shared audio blocks without replicating a downlink stream for every receiver. Yet common reception does not ensure aligned electrical playback, coincident acoustic arrival, or delivery to an entire receiver group. This paper develops a unified feasibility analysis of position-assisted UWB multicast audio that separates clock and actuation error, age-dependent acoustic propagation compensation, correlated block erasures, and reserved communication resources. We derive a conditional bound on one-listener arrival spread, a stationary expression for all-receiver block delivery under common and receiver-local losses, and complementary bounds for reliability-constrained admission. Reproducible Monte Carlo experiments examine 4,590 policy--run records across clock, localization, channel, and slot configurations. For eight receivers, affine clock correction produces a mean run-level 95th-percentile electronic span of $21.19\us$, while position assistance reduces the corresponding one-listener acoustic arrival span from $21.95\ms$ to $419.43\us$. Under the stated $30\us$ timing criterion, 98.86\% of compensated events still exceed the threshold. For 64 receivers, three block copies attain an all-receiver delivery probability of approximately 0.97478 under the modeled correlated channel. The analysis exposes the distinct failure mechanisms of position age, shared fades, retransmission limits, and schedule saturation, and establishes joint criteria for interpreting synchronous multicast audio performance.

papers.title: Proliferation Transitions for Quantum Doubles of Groups
papers.abstract: Proliferation transitions are phase transitions between a 2+1d topological order $\mathcal{T}$ and another $\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{A}$, obtained by condensing anyons in an algebra $\mathcal{A}\subset \mathcal{T}$. We consider such transitions in quantum doubles of groups, $\mathcal{T}=D(G, \omega)$, for finite groups $G$ possibly with three-cocycle $\omega$, for which condensable algebras are fully classified. Given a condensable algebra $\mathcal{A}$, we represent $\mathcal{T}$ in terms of a Symmetry Topological Field Theory (SymTFT), that is tailored to the $\mathcal{A}$ proliferation transition. The SymTFT bulk is constructed from the M\"uger center of the subcategory generated by the algebra, i.e. the category of transparent lines, which can be bosons or fermions. Properties of the transition can then be inferred directly from the algebra classification data. For gauged Landau-Ginzburg (LG*) type transitions, we show that they do not only depend on the anyons in $\mathcal{A}$ through their field content, but the cubic interactions are fixed in terms of the multiplication structure of $\mathcal{A}$. Applied to twin algebras, which have the same anyon content but different multiplication structures, we show that twins result in distinct proliferation transitions.

papers.title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst-case interactions. With GPT-OSS-120B agents on robot routing, a three-agent team finds collision-free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six-agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

papers.title: Learning Normal Coordinates on Riemannian Manifolds with Flow Charts
papers.abstract: Riemannian manifolds are powerful models for problems with non-Euclidean structure. Recent work in geometric machine learning has focused on training deep neural networks to learn Riemannian metrics from high-dimensional data. However, many geometric algorithms require repeated evaluations of the exponential and logarithmic maps, whose high computational cost restricts the utility of learned Riemannian manifolds in practice. We propose to address this cost by training a conditional invertible neural network, called a flow chart, to approximate normal coordinates around points on a given Riemannian manifold. With this approach, the exponential and logarithmic maps can be approximated by fast Euclidean operations in the model's learned coordinate space. Our main contribution is an efficient loss function for training flow charts that is nonnegative and, under suitable domain assumptions, is zero precisely when the chart is normal. Across sixteen synthetic and data-derived geometries, flow charts are competitive with a specialized neural geodesic interpolator for logarithmic map estimation, while also being able to estimate the exponential map. When pretrained, flow charts provide a median speedup of 60-70x over numerical baselines at comparable logarithmic map estimation error, and their learned coordinates improve the accuracy of a numerical geodesic solver.

papers.title: Confessions of a Masked MDP
papers.authors: Sebastian Reboul, Lorenzo Croissant, H\'el\`ene Halconruy
papers.abstract:
In reinforcement learning, one presumes the action set to be known ahead of time, and, thus, one must know if any state-action pairs are not permissible
  ahead of computations. In some applications, determining this action mask is the main computational bottleneck. Isolating this problem to highlight its core
  properties, we study how to combine the search for an optimal policy with the learning of the mask itself, under a linear MDP model in which each attempted
  action reveals the exact value of a linear score determining its validity. In this framework, we first construct an algorithm based on deterministic
  optimistic optimization and show that it is minimax optimal, which we show is also computationally efficient. However, it is sub-optimal on non-degenerate
  instances, as we show. We propose an alternative, which is also computationally efficient, which plans its exploration strategy. This algorithm admits a
  formal interpretation as an analogue of information-directed-sampling for deterministic feedback, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we study an
  application of this framework to transfer learning, where the invalid action set changes over time.

papers.title: A General Construction of Strict Models in HoTT
papers.authors: Niyousha Najmaei, Niels van der Weide
papers.abstract:
Homotopy type theory (HoTT) provides a natural setting for studying the metatheory of type theory, as it comes with additional extensionality principles compared to ordinary Martin-L\"of type theory. In particular, it is especially suitable for developing semantics of type theory, where one distinguishes two kinds of models: strict models, which give us sound interpretations, and pseudomodels. Pseudomodels are useful as they occur prevalently and can be turned into strict models by constructions called strictifications. However, the commonly used strictifications do not translate well to HoTT, as they require assumptions that are generally not satisfied by concrete examples of models.
  We show how to carry out the universe model construction, due to Voevodsky, in HoTT. Under this construction, every pseudomodel together with a universe type closed under enough type formers gives rise to a strict model. We also show how to interpret type formers in the resulting model assuming that the universe is closed under them. Finally, we demonstrate that this construction generalises existing instances of strict set models in the literature, and we apply it to more examples, yielding presheaf models and assembly models of type theory in HoTT. Our results are formalised in Rocq using the UniMath library.

papers.title: Budgeted Admission from Timestamped Capacity Records in Shared Clusters
papers.abstract: A cluster admission gate can receive a capacity record that no longer matches current schedulability. We study one exogenous binary schedulability unit under a bound on the joint probability of admission and unavailability. For a symmetric Markov state, we derive the stationary admission frontier for a fixed observation delay and apply finite likelihood allocation to a delay-tagged delivered record. A one-sided exact binomial endpoint calibrates each fitted policy, and exact enumeration confirms the per-policy confidence target in every tested parameter cell. A separate deterministic guard charges every unresolved admission against the realized allowance and bounds unavailable-state admissions at every prefix under truthful outcome feedback. An executable admission procedure composes the allocation and guard. The controlled system binds source sampling, NATS delivery, randomized admission, Kubernetes objects, and API-derived outcomes in one append-only record. Independent audit finds no missing event, identity mismatch, or state mismatch in the completed functional block. A separate CPU request-accounting check preserves Job and Pod identity across an unschedulable-to-complete transition.

papers.title: Do Neural Models Prefer Their Submodels?
papers.authors: Alvaro Ribot, Yulia Alexandr, Anna Seigal
papers.abstract: A neural model is the set of functions that can be expressed by a given neural network architecture. Neural models contain natural submodels, such as those obtained by setting some neurons to be inactive. We study the geometry of neural models and ask whether they prefer their submodels. By this we mean whether local minimizers of the loss function lie in a given submodel. We introduce a geometric framework to determine if this occurs. For shallow multilayer perceptrons, we show that subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are never preferred. For deep multilayer perceptrons, we give conditions under which subnetworks with inactive hidden neurons are not preferred. For lightning self-attention, lower-rank submodels are usually not preferred, but we identify examples where they are because they lie on a boundary of the model. Our results show that, aside from a few exceptions, preference for submodels cannot be explained by the geometry of the neural model, and must instead come from other sources such as training dynamics.

papers.title: Linear Axiomatization of Linear Differential Equations
papers.abstract: This article presents an axiomatization of linear differential equations that is complete for topologically open properties with compact initial conditions and time horizons by proving them deductively via a sound reduction to formulas of linear real arithmetic. Indeed, linearity is preserved: linear differential invariants are complete for open properties of linear differential equations and reduce with a linear number of Lie derivatives (per atom) to linear real arithmetic. In particular, this article shows that the linear fragment of differential dynamic logic (dL), a modal extension of standard first-order logic over the reals satisfies these completeness properties. By establishing completeness within decidable linear real arithmetic, the need for proving sophisticated nonlinear formulas of real arithmetic is circumvented. Furthermore, this article establishes generalizations to the nonlinear fragment of dL that enable the practical certification of reachability computations, validating the output of external computations in dL with machine-checkable proofs.

papers.title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
papers.abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

papers.title: Geometry-Agnostic Data-Driven Discovery of Extreme Scenarios
papers.authors: Angeline Hu, Ava K. Tse, Kaitlyn S. Yasumura, Luciana Sarabia, Malcolm Yeung, Kavin K. Prasanna, Kai Wong, William Hammond, Ioannis G. Keverkidis, Shengkai Li, Trung V. Phan
papers.abstract: We introduce a two-stage data-driven neural framework for discovering dynamically admissible extreme scenarios. Rather than assuming prior knowledge of the governing equations, the first stage infers the effective dynamical constraints directly from observational data. When the underlying physical system possesses suitable symmetries, the learned dynamics can be represented in a geometry-agnostic form, independent of any fixed grid, coordinate system, dimensionality, and intrinsic curvature. In the second stage, a physics-informed neural-search uses this learned dynamics to uncover rare, high-impact coherent structures that may not have appeared in the original observations. We demonstrate this framework through representative examples of increasing dimensionality and geometric complexity. Starting from a traditionally learned Duffing dynamics, we find a homoclinic pulse as a plausible localized extreme scenario. Next, since the same equation also appears in the stationary nonlinear Schrodinger system, with the coordinate interpreted as space instead of time, this pulse becomes a standing soliton. We then retrain the first stage using a geometry-agnostic neural representation, enabling the learned dynamics to be lifted to higher-dimensional space to obtain higher-dimensional solitary profile, known as Townes soliton. Finally, with a Liouville system, we demonstrate that dynamics learned from data on a (1+1)-dimensional Lorentzian quasi-manifold can be transferred to a (2+0)-dimensional Euclidean manifold to identify an instanton. Our approach can be applied to other coherent spatiotemporal structures, including kinks, rogue waves, compactons, peakons, and potentially even singularities, with applications in risk analysis, nonlinear forecasting, and anomaly detection.

papers.title: Toda chain solves large BKP
papers.abstract: We prove that any solution of the Toda chain hierarchy (the 1D reduction of the 2D Toda lattice) is a solution of the large BKP hierarchy. This is a difference analogue of Alexandrov's result that KdV solves (small) BKP.

papers.title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
papers.authors: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

papers.title: Towards differential expansion for generic representations
papers.abstract: We report the first results of phenomenological analysis, based on extended set of explicitly calculated colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials in \cite{knotebook}. They concern differential expansion (DE), which separates the dependencies on the knot ${\cal K}$ and the representation $R$. %of colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials. DE is well understood for symmetric and rectangular representations, while for non-rectangular $R$ even the knot-independent basis $Z_R^X$ of DE is not known. We concentrate on two issues: the possible derivation of DE and on improved characteristic of its defect. We discuss how evolution families -- twist knots, double braids and 3-pretzels -- can be used to find DE by a peculiar triangular transformation of evolution coefficients. Once $Z^R_X$ are found for particular family, they are expected to stay basically the same for arbitrary knots -- modulo controllable reductions, characterized by the defect of DE, which puts knots into different universality classes. Contrary to original expectation, these classes appear labeled not by a single number $\delta^{\cal K}$, but by a whole non-decreasing sequence $\{k_j\}$, which is squeezed between two staircases, ${\rm entier}\left(\frac{j-1}{\delta+1}\right)\leq k_j\leq{\rm entier}\left(\frac{j-1}{{\rm deg}\,\Delta}\right)$, where the upper bound involves Alexander polynomial $\Delta(q^2)$ and follows from the continuation of the Melvin--Morton--Rozansky-Kashaev limit to $A=q^{-m}$ with $m>0$, when the limit gives a {\it positive} power of Alexander. The old assumption $\delta+1={\rm deg}\,\Delta$ is oversimplified and fails for 19 non-alternating knots with 11 and 12 crossings. Last, we list the differences of non-rectangularly colored HOMFLY for various mutant pairs to demonstrate their universality (knot-independence) and nice consistency with the spirit of DE.

papers.title: Beamfocusing Versus Airy Beams: Does Antenna Blockage Require Beam Bending?
papers.authors: Emil Bj\"ornson, Vitaly Petrov, Erik G. Larsson
papers.abstract: Airy beams are often proposed in array beamforming to bend beams around obstacles. We prove that, for a single-antenna receiver, conventional beamfocusing maximizes the received power regardless of how many antennas are blocked and, in expectation, even with phase errors in the channel state information. This also holds for multi-antenna receivers under a phase-separability condition that is satisfied in rank-one channels. Numerical results confirm that unmodified beamfocusing is optimal for physically small receivers (i.e., those that fit within the beamwidth) when an obstacle is present. For physically larger receivers, the optimal precoding deviates from beamfocusing to better illuminate the receiver's unobstructed parts, but will not become Airy beams. While Airy beams can be configured to perform well, their ability to follow a bent trajectory in front of an obstacle does not maximize the received power behind it.

papers.title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
papers.authors: Gabin Maxime Nguegnang, Bubacarr Bah, Holger Rauhut, Ulrich Terstiege
papers.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings.
