papers.title: Solving Inverse Problems via Diffusion-Based Priors: An Approximation-Free Ensemble Sampling Approach
papers.authors: Haoxuan Chen, Yinuo Ren, Martin Renqiang Min, Lexing Ying, Zachary Izzo
papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be effective in modeling high-dimensional distributions, leading to their widespread adoption for representing complex priors in Bayesian inverse problems (BIPs). However, current DM-based posterior sampling methods proposed for solving common BIPs rely on heuristic approximations to the generative process. To exploit the generative capability of DMs and avoid the usage of such approximations, we propose an ensemble-based algorithm that performs posterior sampling without the use of heuristic approximations. Our algorithm is motivated by existing work that combines DM-based methods with the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method. By examining how the prior evolves through the diffusion process encoded by the pre-trained score function, we derive a modified partial differential equation (PDE) governing the evolution of the corresponding posterior distribution. This PDE includes a modified diffusion term and a reweighting term, which can be simulated via stochastic weighted particle methods. Theoretically, we prove that the error between the true posterior and the empirical distribution of the generated samples can be bounded in terms of the training error of the pre-trained score function and the number of particles in the ensemble. Empirically, we validate our algorithm on several inverse problems in imaging to show that our method gives more accurate reconstructions compared to existing DM-based methods. Our code is available at the following Github repository~\url{https://github.com/HaoxuanSteveC00/AFDPS-TMLR}.

papers.title: Quantitative Quantum Soundness for Bipartite Compiled Bell Games via the Sequential NPA Hierarchy
papers.authors: Igor Klep, Connor Paddock, Marc-Olivier Renou, Simon Schmidt, Lucas Tendick, Xiangling Xu, Yuming Zhao
papers.abstract: Compiling Bell games under cryptographic assumptions replaces the need for physical separation, allowing nonlocality to be probed with a single untrusted device. While Kalai et al. (STOC'23) showed that this compilation preserves quantum advantages, its quantitative quantum soundness has remained an open problem. We address this gap with two primary contributions. First, we establish the first quantitative quantum soundness bounds for all bipartite compiled Bell games via a newly formalized convergent sequential Navascu\'es-Pironio-Ac\'in (NPA) hierarchy: any polynomial-time prover's score is controlled by a finite-level hierarchy value, and finite-level convergence gives a negligible gap to the commuting quantum value, or to the tensor-product quantum value under flat optimality. Second, we develop the sequential NPA hierarchy as a computational tool of independent interest, establishing its convergence and a stopping criterion based on flatness, and identifying its conic dual as a sparse SOS hierarchy.

papers.title: Universal Learning of Nonlinear Dynamics
papers.authors: Evan Dogariu, Anand Brahmbhatt, Elad Hazan
papers.abstract: We study the fundamental problem of one-step prediction of a marginally stable unknown nonlinear dynamical system. We describe an algorithm for this problem, based on the technique of spectral filtering, which learns a mapping from past observations to the next based on a spectral representation of the system. Using techniques from online convex optimization, we prove vanishing prediction error for any nonexpansive nonlinear dynamical system with finitely many marginally stable modes, with rates governed by a novel quantitative control-theoretic notion of learnability. The main technical component of our method is a new spectral filtering algorithm for linear dynamical systems, which incorporates past observations and applies to general noisy and marginally stable systems. This generalizes the original spectral filtering algorithm to both asymmetric dynamics as well as incorporating noise correction, and is of independent interest.

papers.title: Qudit-based scalable quantum algorithm for solving the integer programming problem
papers.authors: Kapil Goswami, Peter Schmelcher, Rick Mukherjee
papers.abstract: Integer programming (IP) is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem that is widely used to represent a diverse set of real-world problems spanning multiple fields, such as finance, engineering, logistics, and operations research. It is a hard problem to solve using classical algorithms, as its complexity increases with problem size. Most quantum algorithms for solving IP are highly resource-inefficient because they encode integers into qubits. In [1], the issue of resource inefficiency was addressed by mapping integer variables to qudits. However, [1] has limited practical value due to a lack of scalability to multiple qudits to encode larger problems. In this work, by extending upon the ideas of [1], a circuit-based scalable quantum algorithm is presented using multiple interacting qudits for which we show a quantum speed-up for solving the integer programming problem. The quantum algorithm consists of a distillation function that efficiently separates the feasible from the infeasible regions, a phase-amplitude encoding for the cost function, and a quantum phase estimation coupled with a multi-controlled single-qubit rotation for optimization. We prove that our algorithm yields the optimal solution with the maximum measurement probability. The time complexity for the quantum algorithm is shown to be $O(r_P(mn^2log d + d^{n/2}/N_{y_s}^{1/2} + n \epsilon_{\text{QPE}}^{-1}))$ for a problem with the number of variables $n$ taking $d$ integer values, satisfying $m$ constraints with a precision of $\epsilon_{\text{QPE}}$ and $r_P$ repetitions required for reaching a success probability $P$. Compared to the classical time complexity of brute force $O(d^n)$ and the classical exact algorithm $O((\log{n})^{O(n)})$, it incurs a reduction of $\sim d^{n/2}$ in the time complexity (for a polynomial number of repetitions and precision requirements) for solving a general polynomial IP problem.

papers.title: Modelling optimal implementation of an arbitrary $N$-qubit quantum gate within the generalized Bloch vectors formalism
papers.abstract: The optimal implementation of quantum gates for closed $N$-qubit systems is one of the key challenges for practical realization of many quantum information processing tasks. In the present article, based on the generalized Bloch vectors formalism [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 54, 195301 (2021)] for a finite-dimensional quantum system, we develop a new general model for the optimal implementation of quantum gates, which is formulated in terms of the Bloch vectors for the unitary evolution operator and the system Hamiltonians, drift and control, and has the unified mathematical form, which is standard for the mathematical control theory and applicable for the implementation of an arbitrary $N$-qubit gate within any closed $N$-qubit system, satisfying the controllability conditions. Within the developed optimal model, the cost functional has both the terminal part and also, the integral part with the special scaling, and this allows us to specify the quantum optimal control synthesis via solving the two-point boundary value problem (BVP) for the system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which can be explored numerically by any of the known BVP solvers for ODEs. The numerical experiments, conducted for the implementation within the developed optimal model of a variety of $N=1,2,3$ qubit gates, demonstrate the high accuracy of the model-based results.

papers.title: Nonlinear Landau levels in the almost-bosonic anyon gas
papers.authors: Alireza Ataei, Ask Ellingsen, Filippa Getzner, Th\'eotime Girardot, Douglas Lundholm, Dinh-Thi Nguyen
papers.abstract: We consider the quantitative description of a many-particle gas of interacting abelian anyons in the plane, confined in a trapping potential. If the anyons are modeled as bosons with a magnetic flux attachment, and if the total magnetic flux is small compared to the number of particles, then an average-field description becomes appropriate for the low-energy collective state of the gas. Namely, by means of a Hartree-Jastrow ansatz, we derive a two-parameter Chern-Simons-Schr\"odinger energy functional which extends the well-known Gross-Pitaevskii / nonlinear Schr\"odinger density functional theory to the magnetic (anyonic) self-interaction. One parameter determines the total number of self-generated magnetic flux units in the system, and the other the effective strength of spin-orbit self-interaction. This latter interaction can be either attractive/focusing or repulsive/defocusing, and depends both on the intrinsic spin-orbit interaction and the relative length scale of the flux profile of the anyons. Densities and energies of ground and excited states are studied analytically and numerically for a wide range of the parameters and align well with a sequence of exact nonlinear Landau levels describing Jackiw-Pi self-dual solitons. With increasing flux, counter-rotating vortices are formed, enhancing the stability of the gas against collapse. Apart from clarifying the relations between various different anyon models that have appeared in the literature, our analysis sheds new light on the many-anyon spectral problem, and also exemplifies a novel supersymmetry-breaking phenomenon.

papers.title: Decentralized Decoding with Adaptive Local Combining for Cell-Free Massive MIMO
papers.authors: Mohd Saif Ali Khan, Karthik RM, Samar Agnihotri
papers.abstract: In existing literature, a two-stage architecture comprising of large-scale fading decoding (LSFD) at the central processing unit (CPU) and local combining at the access points (APs) is commonly deployed for uplink processing in scalable cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (CF-mMIMO) systems. However, centralized LSFD (c-LSFD) requires cross-AP channel statistics at the CPU and local combining uses schemes that either do not suppress interference optimally or result in analytically intractable solutions. We provide novel schemes to address both concerns. First, we propose the decentralized LSFD (d-LSFD) scheme that maximizes a surrogate signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio built only from local interference covariance statistics and identify covariance-action regime where it is equivalent to c-LSFD. Second, based on the fact that the antennas at each AP provide spatial degrees of freedom (DoFs) for both interference suppression and coherent array gain, we interpret every combining scheme as solving the optimal DoF allocation problem over available DoFs. Selective zero-forcing (ZF) schemes solve this problem over both the dimension and composition of the local ZF subspace. We then provide the DoF-adaptive ZF-subspace (DAZS) combining scheme, which lets each AP select the optimal directions in the ZF subspace by maximizing its local sum spectral efficiency. Our numerical results establish the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed schemes compared to the corresponding existing schemes.

papers.title: On the utility problem in a market where price impact is transient
papers.abstract: We consider a discrete-time model of a financial market where a risky asset is bought and sold with transactions having a transient price impact. It is shown that the corresponding utility maximization problem admits a solution. We manage to remove some unnatural restrictions on the market depth and resilience processes that were present in earlier work. A non-standard feature of the problem is that the set of attainable portfolio values may fail the convexity property.

papers.title: Improved exploration of temporal graphs
papers.authors: Paul Bastide, Carla Groenland, Lukas Michel, Cl\'ement Rambaud, Paulina Smolarova
papers.abstract:
A temporal graph $G$ is a sequence $(G_t)_{t \in I}$ of graphs on the same vertex set of size $n$. The \emph{temporal exploration problem} asks for the length of the shortest sequence of vertices that starts at a given vertex, visits every vertex, and at each time step $t$ either stays at the current vertex or moves to an adjacent vertex in $G_t$. When each $G_t$ is connected and has bounded maximum degree, Erlebach, Kammer, Luo, Sajenko, and Spooner [ICALP 2019] showed that an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(n^{7/4})$ time steps.
  We significantly improve this bound by showing that $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\log n})$ time steps suffice. In fact, we prove a more general statement unifying this setting with many others. Let the \emph{average temporal maximum degree} $D$ of $G$ be the average of $\max_{t \in I}d_{G_t}(v)$ over all vertices $v \in V(G)$, where $d_{G_t}(v)$ denotes the degree of $v$ in $G_t$. We show that if each $G_t$ is connected, then an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2}\sqrt{D\log n})$ time steps. This gives the first subquadratic upper bound when the underlying graph has bounded average degree, improving the previous best bounds when it is planar or has bounded treewidth. Our bound is subquadratic already when $D=o(n/\log n)$.
  In addition, we make progress on a recent conjecture of Baguley, G\"{o}bel, Klodt, Skretas, Sylvester, and Zamaraev [SODA 2025]. They conjectured that if $\mu$ is a probability distribution on trees with maximum degree at most $\Delta$ and each $G_t$ is sampled independently from $\mu$, then an exploration exists in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\Delta}n)$ time steps with high probability. We show that there is a temporal exploration of length $\mathcal{O}(\Delta n\log^3 n)$ with high probability. This improves the previous best bound of $\mathcal{O}(n^{3/2})$ and extends to the more general setup of average temporal maximum degree.

papers.title: Dynamic response phenotypes and model discrimination in systems and synthetic biology
papers.abstract: Biological systems encode function not primarily in steady states, but in the structure of transient responses elicited by time-varying stimuli. Overshoots, biphasic dynamics, adaptation kinetics, fold-change detection, entrainment, and cumulative exposure effects often determine phenotypic outcomes, yet are poorly captured by classical steady-state or dose-response analyses. This paper develops an input-output perspective on such "dynamic phenotypes," emphasizing how qualitative features of transient behavior constrain underlying network architectures independently of detailed parameter values. A central theme is the role of sign structure and interconnection logic, particularly the contrast between monotone systems and architectures containing antagonistic pathways. We show how incoherent feedforward (IFF) motifs provide a simple and recurrent mechanism for generating non-monotonic and adaptive responses across multiple levels of biological organization, from molecular signaling to immune regulation and population dynamics. Conversely, monotonicity imposes sharp impossibility results that can be used to falsify entire classes of models from transient data alone. Beyond step inputs, we highlight how periodic forcing, ramps, and integral-type readouts such as cumulative dose responses offer powerful experimental probes that reveal otherwise hidden structure, separate competing motifs, and expose invariances such as fold-change detection. Throughout, we illustrate how control-theoretic concepts, including monotonicity, equivariance, and input-output analysis, can be used not as engineering metaphors, but as precise mathematical tools for biological model discrimination. Thus we argue for a shift in emphasis from asymptotic behavior to transient and input-driven dynamics as a primary lens for understanding, testing, and reverse-engineering biological networks.

papers.title: A Level Set Method on Particle Flow Maps
papers.authors: Jinjin He, Taiyuan Zhang, Zhiqi Li, Junwei Zhou, Duowen Chen, Bo Zhu
papers.abstract: Accurate interface tracking is central to numerical simulations involving moving boundaries, including multiphase flows, free-surface dynamics, phase-change problems, and other interface-driven processes in computational mechanics. Although level set methods provide a flexible implicit representation of evolving interfaces, their grid-based advection and reinitialization procedures often introduce numerical diffusion, volume loss, and degradation of thin or highly curved structures. This paper introduces a Particle Flow Map Level Set (PFM-LS) method that addresses these limitations by transporting interface geometry through particle-carried bidirectional flow maps. In contrast to particle level set methods that use particles mainly as corrective markers, PFM-LS uses particles as primary carriers of level-set values, gradients, and Hessians within a narrow band around the interface. The method combines long-range flow-map transport, high-order particle-grid reconstruction, adaptive particle control, and a hybrid particle-grid redistancing scheme to preserve both signed-distance consistency and sub-grid geometric features. Numerical benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including topology-change tests, chamfer and Hausdorff shape-error metrics, and coupling to an incompressible free-surface flow solver, show that PFM-LS achieves strong volume preservation, high shape fidelity, and near fourth-order convergence, outperforming a broad range of existing level set and reference-map-based methods.

papers.title: Combinatorial properties of holographic entropy inequalities
papers.authors: Guglielmo Grimaldi, Matthew Headrick, Veronika E. Hubeny, Pavel Shteyner
papers.abstract: A holographic entropy inequality (HEI) is a linear inequality obeyed by Ryu-Takayanagi holographic entanglement entropies, or equivalently by the minimum cut function on weighted graphs. We establish a new combinatorial framework for studying HEIs, and use it to prove several properties they share, including two majorization-related properties as well as a necessary and sufficient condition for an inequality to be an HEI. We thereby resolve all the conjectures presented in [arXiv:2508.21823], proving two of them and disproving the other two. In particular, we show that the null reduction of any superbalanced HEI passes the majorization test defined in [arXiv:2508.21823], thereby providing strong new evidence that all HEIs are obeyed in time-dependent holographic states.

papers.title: Madelung hydrodynamics of spin-orbit coupling: action principles, currents, and correlations
papers.abstract: We exploit the variational and Hamiltonian structures of quantum hydrodynamics with spin to unfold the correlation and torque mechanisms accompanying spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in electronic motion. Using Hamilton's action principle for the Pauli equation, we isolate SOC-induced quantum forces that act on the orbital Madelung--Bohm trajectories and complement the usual force terms known to appear in quantum hydrodynamics with spin. While the latter spin-hydrodynamic forces relate to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), SOC-induced orbital forces originate from a particular current operator that contributes prominently to the spin current. This distinction between force terms reveals two fundamentally different mechanisms generating quantum spin-orbit correlations. Leveraging the Hamiltonian structure of the hydrodynamic system, we also elucidate spin transport features such as the correlation-induced quantum torques and the current shift in the spin Hall effect. This Hall shift leads to a new definition of the transport spin current thereby addressing an open question in spintronics. Finally, we illustrate the framework via the Madelung--Rashba equations for planar SOC configurations and propose a particle-based scheme for numerical implementation.

papers.title: Variance Reduction for Stochastic Switching in Functionally Constrained Federated Optimization
papers.authors: Antesh Upadhyay, Sang Bin Moon, Zhankun Luo, Abolfazl Hashemi
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used in safety-critical and fairness-sensitive applications, where learning objectives must be optimized subject to functional constraints. This setting is challenging due to costly projection onto the resulting feasible set, stochastic constraint information, partial client participation, and limited communication at edge devices. We propose a federated stochastic switching framework based on primal-only updates, avoiding dual-variable tuning for functionally constrained federated optimization. For convex objectives, the framework further supports compression with error feedback to control compression-induced bias. We establish high-probability convergence and feasibility guarantees under stochastic gradients and partial client participation, and extend the analysis to weakly convex objectives through proximal-stationarity guarantees. Our bounds isolate the effects of stochastic gradients, constraint-evaluation noise, and partial participation, and show that direct switching can retain a nonvanishing constraint-estimation error even with exact local constraint evaluations. To overcome this limitation, we develop variance-reducing constraint estimators that yield vanishing feasibility and stationarity guarantees with fixed per-round client participation and constraint-evaluation batch sizes. Experiments on Neyman-Pearson classification, fairness-constrained learning on the ADULT dataset, and constrained deep reinforcement learning demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Coherent risk from finite models
papers.abstract: Coherent estimators at different sample sizes need not describe the same population risk. We prove that dyadic estimators do so exactly when duplicating every scenario leaves the estimate unchanged, and recover the population dual set from the finite models. The risk of a Bernoulli loss determines the exact Wasserstein, Kolmogorov and total-variation moduli on a common bounded support. It also characterises uniform estimability, with an impossibility bound for arbitrary randomised estimators. An intrinsic floor on tail levels gives an explicit optimal Lipschitz constant and a uniform approximation defect; every deterministic vanishing floor preserves pointwise strong consistency. A nonstandard construction supplies compatible estimators at all finite sample sizes, explicit block-sum weights, and a formula for the worst-case mass created by infinitesimal tail levels. Finally, we derive uniform regret bounds for data-driven risk-averse optimisation and specialise them to stop-loss retention. Exact binomial calculations compare regularised and original estimators against the same population target.

papers.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees
papers.authors: laf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli
papers.abstract: High-fidelity (HF) simulations of parametric partial differential equations are expensive, whereas low-fidelity (LF) models such as coarse grids or simplified physics are cheap but biased. Multi-fidelity physics-informed neural networks combine the two, yet it remains unclear when cheap physics actually reduces the number of HF solves, and existing methods silently fail when the LF model is misleading and offer no guaranteed uncertainty. We answer the first question with a sharp sample-complexity bound: learning the HF field through its discrepancy from the LF model reduces the number of HF samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by the factor $\kappa^{2\gamma}$, where $\kappa$ is the ratio of the complexity of the discrepancy to that of the HF field and $\gamma$ is the effective-dimension exponent, and we confirm the predicted scaling with exact risk computations in a kernel model. Guided by the analysis, we propose GaMF-PINN, a gated multi-fidelity PINN that learns where to trust the LF model and falls back to physics-only learning where it does not, together with a function-level conformal procedure that returns uncertainty bands containing the entire HF solution with probability at least $1-\alpha$ in finite samples. We release MFPDE-Bench, an open benchmark of paired LF/HF solvers for four parametric PDEs with coarse-grid and simplified-physics LF models. Across MFPDE-Bench, GaMF-PINN reaches the accuracy of a standard HF-PINN with up to 8x fewer HF solves, remains robust when the LF model is deliberately corrupted, and attains the nominal coverage where Bayesian PINNs and deep ensembles under-cover.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Wasserstein Error Bounds and Concentration Inequalities for Nonlinear Stochastic Approximation
papers.abstract: Stochastic approximation methods such as stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning return either the last iterate or the Polyak--Ruppert average. We establish finite-sample Wasserstein-$p$ Gaussian approximation bounds for both outputs under a common framework combining moment bounds for the normalized iterates with quantitative Gaussian approximation of the appropriately weighted driving noise. These bounds yield convergence of admissible moments and high probability bounds with Gaussian leading terms: heavier dependence on the confidence level is confined to a correction that vanishes with the sample size. We verify the framework's conditions for nonlinear stochastic approximation with independent or Markovian observations and linear stochastic approximation with Markovian observations, with applications to stochastic gradient descent and temporal-difference learning.

papers.title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
papers.abstract: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.

papers.title: Trajectory arclength reveals chaos
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the time-averaged phase space arclength of a trajectory, expressed through a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, as a trajectory-based diagnostic for distinguishing regular and chaotic dynamics. The proposed indicator, $\Omega$, is computed by integrating the equations of motion together with a single scalar arclength-accumulation equation and therefore does not require variational equations, neighboring trajectories, or spatial derivatives of a Lagrangian descriptor field. Using Birkhoff's ergodic theorem together with estimates for quasiperiodic motion and correlation-based arguments for chaotic ergodic dynamics, we show that regular and chaotic trajectories exhibit different finite-time behavior despite the convergence of $\Omega$ in both regimes. For quasiperiodic trajectories with Diophantine frequency vectors, deviations from the limiting average decay as $\mathcal{O}(\tau^{-1})$, whereas sufficiently mixing chaotic dynamics exhibit root-mean-square fluctuations of order $\tau^{-1/2}$ under suitable correlation assumptions. This difference in finite-time convergence and fluctuation scaling provides the theoretical basis for using $\Omega$ to discriminate between the two dynamical regimes. We validate the proposed approach in the H\'enon--Heiles and Fermi--Pasta--Ulam systems, comparing the resulting classification of initial conditions with SALI as a reference chaos indicator. The results support $\Omega$ as a complementary single-trajectory diagnostic for chaos detection and as a practical source of scalar features for the analysis of trajectory ensembles, particularly in settings involving large numbers of trajectories or high-dimensional systems.

papers.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
papers.authors: Justin Whitehouse, Ayush Sawarni, Vasilis Syrgkanis
papers.abstract:
The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. In model-agnostic settings, SHAP uses the concept of Shapley values from cooperative game theory to fairly allocate credit to the features in a vector $X$ based on their contribution to an outcome $Y$. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. However, despite their ubiquity, there do not exist approaches for performing statistical inference on these quantities.
  In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. We complement these results by presenting a Neyman orthogonal loss that can be used to learn the SHAP curve via empirical risk minimization and discussing excess risk guarantees for commonly used function classes.

papers.title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
papers.authors: Kelly L Vomo-Donfack, Adryel Hoszu, Gr\'egory Ginot, Ian Morilla
papers.abstract: Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.

papers.title: Synthetic Differential Geometry in Lean
papers.abstract: This article is about the formalization of synthetic differential geometry with the Lean proof assistant and the mathematical library mathlib. The main result we prove and formalize is a Taylor theorem for functions of several variables, where the series expansion is around an infinitesimal neighborhood. Most of our proofs are in fact new. Our investigations highlight the possibility of using mathlib to do constructive mathematics.

papers.title: Quotient Geometry and Persistence-Stable Metrics for Swarm Configurations
papers.abstract: Can temporal information recover geometry lost by a persistence diagram? For $n\ge3$ points on the unit sphere evolving under known homogeneous complete consensus, we prove generic local recovery modulo rotations and permutations from two ordinary zero-dimensional Vietoris--Rips persistence snapshots. The structural result applies to every labeled tree: its edge inner products and their first temporal derivatives have differential rank $2n-3$, exactly the dimension of the regular formation quotient. An explicit pole--equator witness proves this simultaneously for all tree types after taking a finite intersection of open dense sets. Although one snapshot has generic local fibers of dimension $n-2$, two sufficiently close snapshots are injective on a common neighborhood. The optimal inverse Lipschitz constant grows as $\Theta(1/|h|)$ when the sampling interval tends to zero. A verified left inverse, interval derivative bounds, and explicit persistence-matching margins certify neighborhoods and time intervals at rational reference formations. The results are local and model-specific; reflection ambiguity and centered rank obstructions remain.

papers.title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods
papers.authors: Rustem Islamov, Roman Machacek, Aurelien Lucchi, Antonio Silveti-Falls, Eduard Gorbunov, Volkan Cevher
papers.abstract: We study the role of batch size in stochastic conditional gradient methods under a $\mu$-Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz ($\mu$-KL) condition. Focusing on momentum-based stochastic conditional gradient algorithms (e.g., Scion), we derive a new analysis that explicitly captures the interaction between stepsize, batch size, and stochastic noise. Our study reveals a regime-dependent behavior: increasing the batch size initially improves optimization accuracy but, beyond a critical threshold, the benefits saturate and can eventually degrade performance under a fixed token budget. Notably, the theory predicts the magnitude of the optimal stepsize and aligns well with empirical practices observed in large-scale training. Leveraging these insights, we derive principled guidelines for selecting the batch size and stepsize, and propose an adaptive strategy that increases batch size and sequence length during training while preserving convergence guarantees. Experiments on NanoGPT are consistent with the theoretical predictions and illustrate the emergence of the predicted scaling regimes. Overall, our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding batch size scaling in stochastic conditional gradient methods and offer guidance for designing efficient training schedules in large-scale optimization.

papers.title: Tiny but uniform improvements of adaptive BH procedures via compound e-values
papers.authors: Nikolaos Ignatiadis, Ruodu Wang, Aaditya Ramdas
papers.abstract: After the seminal Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) was proposed, dozens of papers have attempted to improve its power by adapting to the unknown proportion of nulls. We observe that most null-proportion estimates are simply compound e-values in disguise, and thus most adaptive FDR procedures can be interpreted as instances of the e-weighted BH (ep-BH) procedure of Ignatiadis, Wang, and Ramdas [2024], i.e., the BH procedure weighted by compound e-values. This lens helps us show that most existing procedures are inadmissible, and we provide uniform improvements to them. While the improvements are small in practice, they still come for free (without additional assumptions), and help unify the literature. We also use our "leave-one-out ep-BH method" to design a new method with finite-sample FDR control for the simultaneous t-test setting.

papers.title: Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: Formal model evaluation methods typically certify that a model satisfies a prescribed target key performance indicator (KPI) level. However, in many applications, the relevant target KPI level may not be known a priori, and the user may instead wish to compare candidate models by analyzing the full trade-offs between performance and reliability achievable at test time by the models. This task, requiring the reliable estimate of the test-time KPI distributions, is made more complicated by the fact that the same data must often be used both to pre-select a subset of candidate models and to estimate their KPI distributions, causing a potential post-selection bias. In this work, we introduce post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a general framework for statistically valid distributional model assessment after arbitrary data-dependent model pre-selection. Building on e-values, PS-DME controls post-selection false coverage rate (FCR) for the distributional KPI estimates and we establish explicit conditions under which it is provably more sample efficient than a baseline method based on sample splitting. Experiments on synthetic data, text-to-SQL decoding with large language models, and telecom network performance evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME enables reliable comparison of candidate configurations across a range of reliability levels, supporting the statistically reliable exploration of performance--reliability trade-offs.

papers.title: Boundary R\'enyi oscillations in the open XX chain
papers.abstract: For the ground state of the semi-infinite XX chain with Fermi momentum $k_F$, we derive the extracted $2k_F$ contribution to the R\'enyi entropy of its first $\ell$ sites at fixed $\alpha>1$. Its phase $\sin[(2\ell+1)k_F]$ matches the Friedel oscillation at the entangling bond and becomes the even--odd alternation at half filling. An exact Hankel determinant reduction and Riemann--Hilbert analysis give every term $\mathcal{L}^{-(2q-1)/\alpha}$ for positive integers $q$ with $2q-1<\alpha$, where $\mathcal{L}=4\ell\sin k_F$, with an $O(\mathcal{L}^{-1})$ error within this extracted component for $k_F$ away from $0$ and $\pi$. At integer $\alpha=p\ge2$, exact factorization gives a finite sum over all roots with error $O(\mathcal{L}^{-1-1/p})$. We also determine the $2k_F$ terms of $\log Z_\alpha(\phi)$, where $Z_\alpha(\phi)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_A^\alpha e^{i\phi Q_A})$, $\rho_A$ is the block's reduced density matrix, and $Q_A$ is its fermion number. At fixed nonzero flux $|\phi|<\pi$ with $2q-1\mp\phi/\pi\ne\alpha$, the two exponential terms have different decay powers. Exact factorization sharpens the integer result. These pointwise estimates do not justify projection to fixed charge. The uncharged sequence and the two leading charged terms agree with earlier generalized Fisher--Hartwig predictions. Numerical calculations at $p=4$ test the predicted subleading coefficients without an adjustable normalization.

papers.title: A Transport Geometry of Benign Overfitting
papers.authors: Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli
papers.abstract: Benign overfitting, the phenomenon that interpolating noisy data can be statistically harmless, is usually characterized through effective-rank conditions on the covariance spectrum. These conditions are fragile: a perturbation of vanishing relative operator and Frobenius norm can turn a benign covariance into one whose minimum-norm interpolator has non-vanishing excess risk. We argue that the natural geometry of benign overfitting is optimal transport of the log-eigenvalues, measured in units of the sample size $n$. In log-spectral coordinates, the deterministic equivalent of the risk becomes a functional of two measures smoothed by a logistic kernel centred at the interpolation threshold $\log\kappa$. We compute its exact first variation: the threshold moves by a sensitivity-weighted average of the log-eigenvalue displacements, and the influence of each eigenvalue decays exponentially with its log-distance to the threshold. We then derive global, dimension-free stability bounds. The variance functional is $8/(27n)$-Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance between log-spectra, with a sharp constant, and is controlled more generally by a threshold-localized transport discrepancy; an analogous bound controls the bias. Consequently, any rank-$k$ update of the covariance, of arbitrary norm, changes the variance functional by at most $3k/n$, and benign overfitting survives every perturbation whose localized transport cost is $o(n)$. The results extend to ridge regression and to infinite-dimensional trace-class covariances. Matching lower bounds show that the $n$-scaling is necessary and cannot be replaced by operator norms, Frobenius norms, or dimension-normalized spectral distances. Simulations, one-step feature learning in two-layer networks, and random features of real images support the theory and delineate its limits.

papers.title: Beyond the Flat-Spike: Adaptive Sparse CCA for Decaying and Unbalanced Signals
papers.authors: Mengchu Xu, Jian Wang, Yonina C. Eldar
papers.abstract: Sparse Canonical Correlation Analysis (SCCA) is a fundamental statistical tool for identifying linear relationships in high-dimensional, multi-view data. While minimax theory establishes an optimal sample complexity scaling additively with the sparsity levels of the canonical vectors, computationally efficient algorithms typically suffer from a suboptimal multiplicative dependence. This computational-statistical gap is intrinsically tied to worst-case ``flat'' signal assumptions. In practice, however, multi-view signals frequently exhibit structured energy concentration, such as a power-law decay. To exploit this structural concentration and bypass the worst-case bottleneck, we propose Bilateral Spectral Energy Pursuit (Bi-SEP). Operating directly on the cross-covariance matrix, Bi-SEP is a stagewise adaptive algorithm that utilizes a proxy refinement step to dynamically track and capture cross-view signal energy. Theoretically, we establish a profile-adaptive sample complexity bound governed by the coupled energy profiles of the two views. Notably, under power-law decay models, we reveal a synergistic phase transition: the optimal linear sample complexity is attainable provided that the aggregate decay rate of the two views is sufficiently large. This result demonstrates that a highly concentrated signal in one view allows the model to accommodate a completely flat signal in its partner. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings, illustrating the advantages of Bi-SEP in structured, non-flat signal regimes.

papers.title: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Pearl's causal hierarchy shows that observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries are qualitatively distinct. We ask a quantitative version of this question: how many additional bits are needed to specify higher-rung causal answers once lower-rung answers are known? We formalize this via query-class description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of the answers a structural causal model (SCM) gives to a class of queries, with system size given. Our main construction gives acyclic SCMs on $n$ binary variables whose common observational distribution has constant description length, while single-variable intervention answers can require $\Theta(n^2)$ additional bits. For SCMs with independent noises, fixed finite gate-schema and noise libraries, and at most $d$ parents per variable, a degree-sensitive upper bound gives an observational-interventional gap of at most $O(nd\log(en/d)+n\log n)$. This makes the quadratic construction order-optimal in the dense regime and a rooted-tree construction order-optimal for bounded indegree. The quadratic separation persists under $\varepsilon$-accurate total-variation descriptions for every fixed $\varepsilon<1/4$. At the next rung, even knowing every hard-intervention distribution can leave a $\Theta(n)$ counterfactual description gap; a masked-parity construction extends this to $\Theta(n^2)$. These separation rates hold in the worst case and with high probability under uniform hidden parameters. A general ambiguity-to-bits theorem and Shannon analogue, together with explicit encodings, show that the gaps in our constructions equal the logarithm of residual higher-rung ambiguity up to lower-order terms.

papers.title: Dynamic Quantum-Assisted Co-Design of Controller and Lyapunov Candidate Parameters for Nonlinear Systems
papers.authors: Milad Hasanzadeh, Amin Kargarian, Mehdi Farasat
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a dynamic quantum-assisted co-design framework for nonlinear closed-loop systems in which controller parameters and Lyapunov candidate parameters are redesigned jointly at successive decision epochs. Unlike conventional nonlinear control designs that typically tune controller gains offline and perform stability analysis separately, the proposed method embeds performance improvement and sample-based Lyapunov verification within a unified online optimization loop. The main novelty is a two-step computational structure that first contracts the continuous admissible search region around the current operating condition using a Black-Hole calibration procedure and then constructs a finite binary representation only over this calibrated region. The encoded objective is obtained from sampled nonlinear closed-loop evaluations and approximated by a local quadratic pseudo-Boolean surrogate, enabling an Ising-type Hamiltonian representation suitable for quantum-assisted optimization. Quantum imaginary time evolution is then used to explore the encoded Hamiltonian, and the resulting candidate bitstrings are decoded into continuous controller and Lyapunov parameters. To reduce dependence on the surrogate model, the decoded candidates are re-evaluated using the original nonlinear closed-loop cost and Lyapunov penalties before the final update is applied. The framework can accommodate sampled forms of different Lyapunov decay specifications by modifying the corresponding penalty and is numerically evaluated on first-order nonlinear consensus, second-order nonlinear consensus, and induction motor drive control examples. The implementation code used to generate the reported results is available at \href{https://github.com/LSU-RAISE-LAB/DQCLS-NS}{GitHub}.

papers.title: Algebraic Structure of Finite-Size Bethe Solutions in the Heisenberg Chain
papers.authors: Oliver R. Bellwood, William J. Munro
papers.abstract: The spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic chain is the canonical example of an integrable quantum many-body model. Despite its exact solvability, explicit finite-size solutions are typically only accessible via numerical evaluation of the Bethe ansatz equations. Here, we analyse the algebraic structure of the exact, symbolic ground states for chains up to twelve sites using the Bethe ansatz. We find that the algebraic degree of the ground state magnon phases and Bethe roots scale with respect to system size at a different rate to the ground-state energy and wavefunction coefficients. The ground-state Bethe roots and energy are found to become Galois unsolvable for ten or more sites, thus demonstrating the lack of a symbolic analytical solution in a quantum integrable model due to algebraic complexity.

papers.title: Cellwise and Casewise Robust Multivariate Regression with Inference
papers.authors: Fabio Centofanti, Mia Hubert, Peter J. Rousseeuw
papers.abstract: Multivariate linear regression is a fundamental statistical task, but classical estimators such as ordinary least squares are highly sensitive to outliers. These may occur as casewise outliers that affect entire observations, or as outlying cells, that are individual contaminated entries in the predictor and/or response matrix. Moreover, modern datasets frequently contain missing values and are high-dimensional. To address these challenges we propose the cellwise multivariate regression (cellMR) estimator, a robust regression method that simultaneously accommodates casewise and cellwise outliers, missing data, and high dimensionality. The approach builds on a cellwise robust covariance estimator and uses ridge regularization for numerical stability. We further introduce cellBoot, a novel bootstrap-based inference procedure tailored to the cellMR framework. Relying on indirect inference, cellBoot provides asymptotically valid confidence intervals that are robust to casewise and cellwise contamination. We derive influence functions and breakdown bounds of the regression estimator and prove the asymptotic validity of the cellBoot confidence intervals. Simulations and a real genomics application illustrate the strong finite-sample performance of the proposed methods.

papers.title: SPLIT: SymPathy for Large jobs Improves Tail latency
papers.authors: Zhouzi Li, Mor Harchol-Balter, Alan Scheller-Wolf
papers.abstract:
We study the asymptotic response time tail in the M/G/n multi-server queue with heavy-tailed (regularly varying) job sizes, a setting representative of modern computing workloads. For single-server systems, tail optimization is well understood: under heavy-tailed job sizes, policies such as SRPT that strictly prioritize short jobs are strongly tail optimal, and giving any priority to large jobs is harmful. For multi-server systems, the question has been almost entirely open.
  This paper gives the first strongly tail-optimal scheduling policies for the M/G/n queue with heavy-tailed job sizes. Our central finding is that the multi-server case is intrinsically different from the single-server case: giving a small amount of ``sympathy'' to large jobs is essential for strong tail optimality. We establish strong (or arbitrarily close to strong) tail optimality across the full stability region, both with and without knowledge of job sizes.

papers.title: Quantum geometry of connected state manifolds: When diabolic points act as bridges between eigenstate manifolds
papers.authors: Jan St\v{r}ele\v{c}ek, Jakub Novotn\'y, Pavel Cejnar
papers.abstract: Parametric Hamiltonians often exhibit point-like spectral degeneracies, called diabolic points (DPs) or conical intersections, which can lead to singularities in the Provost-Vallee metric of eigenstate manifolds. We regularise the metric by a transformation to polar coordinates and develop a formalism in which DPs act as bridges between adjacent eigenstate manifolds, glueing them into a single connected state manifold (CSM). We characterise the topology of this structure and extend the local rules for nodal lines governing the Berry phase to global ones. On the CSM, the class of geodesics can be enlarged by those passing through the DPs. They can be stable with respect to their initial direction, and can be shorter than those constrained to a single eigenstate manifold, providing new geodesic shortcuts. Further, the CSM provides a new mechanism for Berry phase computation along paths traversing the DPs.

papers.title: New Exotic Operators in the Spectrum of Wilson Lines in General Representations
papers.authors: Daniele Artico, Carlo Meneghelli, Michele Savi, Rudolfs Treilis
papers.abstract: Wilson lines are fundamental probes of gauge theories. We show that, in sufficiently rich representations, they support a large new class of operator insertions. For half-BPS lines in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, some have the quantum numbers of the displacement supermultiplet and define natural defect deformations. By relating their beta-functions to chiral ring OPE coefficients, we show that these deformations are marginally irrelevant, meaning the half-BPS line is IR stable for all representations. We connect these deformations to multidimensional RG flows and find evidence for new conformal line defects.

papers.title: A short proof of a quadratic lower bound on the border determinantal complexity of $x_1^n+\cdots+x_n^n$ over $\mathbb{C}$: A simple human exposition
papers.abstract:
I give a short proof that the border determinantal complexity of $F_n=x_1^n+\cdots+x_n^n$ over $\mathbb{C}$ is at least $(n-1)^2/(4e)$, and at least $(n-1)^2/(2e)$ in the symmetric model. The same argument shows that the border determinantal complexity of $x_1^d+\cdots+x_N^d$ is $\Theta(Nd)$ for all $N\ge3$ and $d\ge2$.
  The earlier article arXiv:2606.13628, by the same author, introduced the first superlinear lower bounds and includes verification by Lean formalization. However, the AI written exposition was hard to follow. Kumar and Volk (arXiv:2609.34462) give a short proof of the exact ordinary case, but do not address the border or symmetric cases. In this article, I provide a greatly simplified exposition of the border and symmetric cases, using the implicit function theorem and an explicit section of simple solutions in place of the conormal specialization arguments of arXiv:2606.13628. I choose an explicit polynomial system with $n(n-1)^{n-2}$ simple solutions for $F_n$. I then use the implicit function theorem to ensure that each point persists under small perturbations. Finally, kernel equations and the multihomogeneous B\'ezout theorem bound the number of these points for a small determinant.
  The exposition is due to the human author. The mathematical simplification was obtained in discussion with ChatGPT Astra and refined in conversation with Claude Opus 5.5.

papers.title: A Decision-Theoretic View of Test-Time Training: When, How Far, and Which Directions to Adapt
papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) adapts a pretrained model to each prompt via parameter updates, improving accuracy under pretraining-to-test distribution shifts. Yet, its performance often suffers from instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters such as update steps and subspace. We explain this behavior through a decision-theoretic lens, treating TTT as implicit Bayesian inference in the kernel regime. Under a Gaussian process benchmark, we show that TTT reduces prediction error when updates are spectrally matched to the prompt's signal-to-noise ratio and aligned with query-relevant eigen-directions. This perspective underpins the following results: (1) we show when fixed update steps and subspaces fail under distribution shifts, motivating adaptive strategies; (2) we prove that selecting update steps via prompt evidence admits a PAC-Bayes guarantee against overfitting; and (3) we characterize the Bayes-optimal update subspace under a linear-Gaussian correction model, yielding a scoring rule for selecting Transformer blocks and heads. Our theory helps explain the empirical instability of TTT, taking a step toward principled guidance for when, how far, and which directions to adapt.

papers.title: All-out Attack: Optimal Block Withholding Under Pay-Per-Share Scheme
papers.abstract: Classical Block Withholding (BWH) attacks have been extensively studied in block-dependent reward schemes, where pool members are compensated upon a block discovery within the pool. However, most contemporary mining pools operate under share-based schemes, wherein participants are paid immediately upon submission of valid shares. In this paper, we analyze BWH under Pay-Per-Share (PPS) for Nakamoto-style blockchains and prove that these mechanisms are not incentive compatible, contrary to conclusions drawn under fixed difficulty in prior literature. Under PPS, the optimal strategy for a BWH attacker is the All-out Attack (AoA): the adversary allocates its entire hashpower toward the victim pool, submitting only partial Proof-of-Work shares (pPoW) while withholding all valid blocks, i.e., full Proof-of-Work (fPoW). Prior to the first difficulty adjustment, the adversary incurs negligible loss from withheld fPoWs. After the adjustment reduces block difficulty, the adversary either generates more pPoWs per unit time when the pPoW difficulty is reduced accordingly or, if the pPoW difficulty is held fixed, earns a higher reward per share. In both cases, it achieves a post-adjustment reward rate of $\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$ per target epoch, compared with the honest baseline rate of $\alpha$. Remarkably, this gain matches the theoretical upper bound achieved by optimal selfish mining in Nakamoto consensus under perfect network influence. The results further indicate that BWH is substantially more profitable under PPS than under mainstream block-dependent payout schemes, even when compared with advanced BWH variants. Honest miners benefit at the same rate as the adversary per unit hashpower, while the victim pool operator bears all losses, paying out-of-pocket for pPoW submissions without receiving fPoW compensation in return.

papers.title: Congestion Games with Heterogeneous Valuations: An Optimal Transport Approach
papers.authors: Pan-Yang Su, Negar Mehr, Shankar Sastry
papers.abstract: In emerging urban mobility and logistics applications, such as advanced air mobility, electric vehicle charging, and shared service systems, agents with heterogeneous valuations choose among multiple outcomes while sharing congested resources. Existing congestion game and resource-allocation models, however, typically restrict either the structure of heterogeneous outcome preferences or the form of congestion externalities. We introduce a nonatomic congestion game framework in which agents have multidimensional heterogeneous valuations over a finite set of outcomes, with the population represented by a measure over the valuation space. We show that, although there is a continuum of heterogeneous agents, both Nash equilibria and social optima admit finite-dimensional characterizations. Nash equilibria are characterized by aggregate flows and outcome-level threshold vectors, while social optima admit a semi-discrete optimal transport formulation characterized by aggregate flows and strategy-level Kantorovich dual potentials. For separable utilities and latency functions $\ell_e$ such that $x\mapsto x\ell_e(x)$ is convex for every resource $e$, the social welfare problem becomes a convex optimization problem, and we characterize social optima through marginal congestion costs and capacity-dual prices. Our results provide a geometric characterization of congestion games with multidimensional heterogeneous valuations and connect nonatomic congestion games with semi-discrete optimal transport.

papers.title: Decoupling Limit of Quiver Theories and the Angular Spectra of Extreme C-metrics
papers.abstract: We investigate the angular eigenvalue problem of the extreme charged C-metric. Starting from a constrained five-point Fuchsian description of the non-extremal angular equation, we obtain its extreme limit by decoupling a hypermultiplet in the dual four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$, $\mathrm{SU(2)}\times \mathrm{SU(2)}$ linear quiver gauge theory. We derive the parameter dictionary and renormalized Matone relations, and connect the physical limit $Q\to M$ to the quiver decoupling by an explicit coordinate transformation. Regular endpoint conditions give an algebraic quantization condition. Eigenvalues obtained from the truncated instanton prepotential are tested against independent angular spectra near extremality and at larger acceleration. The axisymmetric sector recovers the known exact spectrum.

papers.title: Tropical Circuits with Scalar Multiplication Gates
papers.abstract: We study tropical circuits with scalar multiplication gates, that is, algebraic circuits whose gates implement $\max$, $+$, or multiplication with a positive constant. For such circuits, we prove exponential size lower bounds for computing maximum weight directed spanning trees and maximum weight bipartite perfect matchings. As a corollary, we obtain an exponential size separation between monotone and non-monotone maxout neural networks, which generalize the popularly used ReLU neural networks. One conclusion from this is that neural network models with enforced convexity constraints, such as input-convex neural networks (ICNNs), sometimes need to be exponentially larger than their unrestricted counterparts in order to express the same functions.

papers.title: Microstructure-Conditioned Surrogate Models for Graded Multiscale Optimization of Mycelium Composites
papers.authors: J. Storm, I. B. C. M. Rocha, S. Schyck, K. Masania, F. P. van der Meer
papers.abstract: Emerging sustainable materials increasingly rely on engineered hierarchy and microstructure to achieve control of their properties and mechanical behavior. Optimizing these materials with controllable microstructures requires efficient multiscale simulations. Data-driven surrogate models for the microscale can accelerate multiscale simulations, but require large amounts of data even for a fixed microstructure. When a range of microstructures is considered, as is the case in multiscale optimization, even more data is needed to train a surrogate. To overcome this challenge, we condition a hybrid physics-data surrogate on microstructural variables using a hypernetwork. This approach enables accurate predictions of multiscale mechanical behavior for a mycelium-woodchip composite material, even when trained on small datasets. The conditioned surrogate makes multiscale simulations of functionally graded structures tractable, and we validate it against a full FE^2 simulation. We optimize a graded multiscale disk, and reduce the peak stress by 43% compared to one with a random microstructure. Then, we go one step further, conditioning the network directly on manufacturing variables that can have a complex influence on the microstructure. This is a practical route to engineer the microscale for desired macroscale behavior. This contribution highlights the benefits of microarchitectured structures and demonstrates how conditioned surrogate models enable their multiscale optimization, which will accelerate the development and design of future sustainable materials and structures.

papers.title: Reasoning about Continuous-Variable Quantum Systems
papers.authors: Tianshi Yu, Gilles Barthe, Minbo Gao, Mingsheng Ying, Li Zhou
papers.abstract:
Continuous-variable quantum computing (CVQC) is a computing paradigm in which measurements yield values over a continuous domain. CVQC is both a convenient computational framework for modeling physical quantum systems, and a good abstraction for hardware platforms based on quantum optics. Yet, the semantic foundations of CVQC remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we develop a formal semantics for a core CV quantum programming language, and sound verification methods for program correctness.
  A main contribution of this work is to isolate a well-behaved quantitative predicate domain that achieves sufficient expressiveness to accommodate unbounded values as they arise in the infinite-dimensional, continuous setting. Specifically, we choose closed positive quadratic forms as semantic predicates, representing finite expectations, domains of finiteness, and infinite penalties in one ordered object. We validate our choice by establishing that our semantic predicates satisfy desirable closure properties including the definition of weakest preconditions.
  We validate our design with two case studies, including an example based on the celebrated GKP error-correcting code, for which we establish a second moment bound.

papers.title: Geometric $(1+\varepsilon)$-Spanners with Few Crossings
papers.abstract: For $n$ points in the plane and $\varepsilon>0$, we construct a $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner with $O(n/\varepsilon)$ edges in which every edge has $\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^3)$ crossings, the total number of crossings is $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^4)$, and the ratio between the lengths of any two crossing edges is $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$. Our spanner construction substantially improves on the previous upper bound for the number of crossings in a $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner, and it is the first spanner construction that ensures $O(1)$ crossings per edge for any constant $\varepsilon>0$. In contrast, we construct $n$ points in the plane for which every $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner has $\Omega(n/\varepsilon^3)$ crossings, $n$ points for which every $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner has an edge with $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{5/2})$ crossings, and 4 points for which every $(1+\varepsilon)$-spanner contains two crossing edges where one is $\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$ times longer than the other.

papers.title: Odd-even dichotomy in the waveforms of modified Emden oscillators of arbitrary integer power
papers.authors: J. de la Cruz, H. C. Rosu
papers.abstract: Closed-form waveforms of the modified Emden oscillators $\ddot x+(q+2)kx^q\dot x+k^2x^{2q+1}+\omega^2x=0$ of arbitrary natural power $q$, and of their damped $c$-deformed versions, are obtained through a generalized commutative factorization that reduces them to Bernoulli equations. We show that commutative factorizations of Li\'enard equations are gauge-conjugated forms of the nonlocal linearizing transformation of Chandrasekar, Senthilvelan, Kundu and Lakshmanan, the factorization constant being half the difference of the roots of the associated linear oscillator. These oscillators display an odd--even dichotomy: for odd $q$ they are isochronous, with period $2\pi/\omega$ independent of the amplitude, within an explicitly bounded range of the integration constant, while for even $q$ the oscillations decay algebraically, as $t^{-1/q}$. The dichotomy is confirmed by an elliptic polar representation, in which the phase rotates uniformly for every $q$, and, for even $q$, by the Bendixson--Dulac criterion applied to the divergence of the vector field. We present a dissipative Lagrangian of Lurie--Rayleigh type and, for $q=1$, an autonomous Sundman linearization that yields a rational first integral, a Jacobi last multiplier and a non-dissipative Lagrangian; for every $q$, $\omega^2x^2+(\dot x+kx^{q+1})^2$ is a Darboux polynomial providing a global Jacobi last multiplier. Explicit waveforms and phase portraits are given for $q=1,\dots,4$, with and without damping, and a recent application to magnon dynamics in the magnetic semiconductor CrSBr is discussed.

papers.title: Online Discrepancy for Sub-Exponential Product Distributions via Regularization
papers.abstract:
We study online discrepancy minimization for independent random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with independent coordinates. Our deterministic algorithms require no knowledge of the horizon, and their guarantees hold at every prescribed deterministic terminal time $T$. For unit-variance sub-exponential coordinates with $\psi_1$-norms at most $\sigma$, we obtain terminal discrepancy $O(\sigma^4\sqrt n)$ with failure probability $\exp(-\Omega(\sigma^3\sqrt n))$. Independently masking centered unit-variance marks from the same class with retention probability $k/n$ gives $O(\sigma^4\sqrt k)$ discrepancy with failure probability $\exp(-\Omega(\sigma^3\sqrt k))$ when $k\gtrsim\log^2(2n)$. The fourth-power dependence on $\sigma$ is necessary for these sub-exponential classes at the stated confidence levels.
  For standard Gaussian marks, we obtain $O(\sqrt k+\sqrt{\log(2n)})$ discrepancy with failure probability $\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt k+\sqrt{\log(2n)}))$. Both terms are necessary up to absolute constants for $T\ge n$. In particular, $k\gtrsim\log n$ is the optimal sparsity threshold for $O(\sqrt k)$ discrepancy. For centered unit-variance sub-Gaussian marks with any fixed $\psi_2$-norm bound $\sigma$, logarithmic sparsity suffices for $O(\sigma\sqrt{k\log(e+\sigma)})$ discrepancy with probability tending to one as $n\to\infty$. For a dimension-dependent family of unit-variance laws with rare activations, matching bounds determine the fixed-confidence online discrepancy order $\Theta(\sqrt n\log\log n)$ at sufficiently long prescribed horizons.
  Our dense result generalizes the Rademacher-input theorem of Bansal and Spencer (2020) and establishes the horizon-independent $O(\sqrt n)$ Gaussian terminal discrepancy scale anticipated by Gamarnik et al. (2022). The proofs combine regularization, global Fenchel estimates, coupled Lyapunov functions, and terminal moment recursions.

papers.title: Characterizing Client-Independent Stationary Bias for SCAFFOLD and FedAvg in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Even when all clients optimize the same strongly convex objective, the global model parameters produced by constant-step federated learning may still have a stationary mean that differs from the minimizer. Does increasing the number of clients eliminate this bias, or can some components persist? Answering this question clarifies the limits of client averaging. To this end, we study two federated learning algorithms, \Scaf{} and matched \FedAvg{}, under full participation, a sufficiently smooth objective, and independent bounded additive gradient noise. Analyzing global stationary balance and within-round local fluctuations yields multidimensional expansions with a shared $\gamma/N$ term and explicit client-independent $\gamma^2$ coefficients, where $\gamma$ is the step size and $N$ is the client count. The \Scaf{} coefficient combines the ordinary local-update contribution found in \FedAvg{} with an additional persistent-control contribution. Although zero-sum controls cancel from the direct server increment, they change local second moments, which interact with third-order curvature to shift the stationary mean. For fixed dimension $d$ and local-step count $H$, a remainder of $O_{H,d}(\gamma^2/N+\gamma^3)$, uniform in $N$ for sufficiently small $\gamma$, identifies the second-order coefficients along arbitrary joint small-step, large-client limits after removing the shared leading term. Controlled experiments assess the predicted coefficients. In real-data analyses, finite-tail mean displacement can account for a substantial share of averaged-model parameter error, and a post-hoc comparison shows directional agreement with the derived curvature--noise structure.

papers.title: Same path, different walk: a mechanistic comparison of looped and stacked transformer encoders on 12-lead ECG
papers.authors: Pawel Olszowiec, Michal Byra, Grzegorz Gruszczynski, Grzegorz Stefanski, Alberto Presta
papers.abstract: Recurrent Transformers reusing their weights rather than stacking $L$ distinct layers are becoming widely adopted due to their parameter efficiency [1,2,3]. However, the exact representational and dynamical differences between looped and stacked architectures remain uncharacterized. This paper presents a controlled study on the example of bViT model [1] applying one weight-tied block $L$ times. We train two models: bViT and standard ViT [4] on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) classification tasks from the PTB-XL dataset under identical training protocols. Despite an $8.9\times$ parameter reduction, bViT achieves accuracy parity with ViT. Geometric similarity metrics demonstrate that both architectures construct comparable latent representations in an equivalent canonical order. Crucially, their dynamics differ: bViT exhibits smaller step sizes and inter-patient sensitivity, as well as near-neutral behavior away from the data manifold, whereas ViT exhibits collapsing dimensionality of representations and out-of-distribution feature expansion.

papers.title: A sharp norm inequality for entanglement-breaking channels
papers.abstract: For a channel $\Phi$ on $M_d$ written in the generalised Bloch parameterisation $r \mapsto Ar+c$, we prove that entanglement breaking implies $\|A\|_*^2 + \frac{d(d-1)}{2}\,|c|^2 \;\le\; (d-1)^2 ,$ where $\|\cdot\|_*$ denotes the nuclear norm. Read on the Choi state of the channel, the inequality is an instance of the covariance-matrix criterion of Gittsovich et al.; what is added here is an elementary proof in Holevo form and a complete description of the equality cases. Apart from the constant channel onto a pure state, which shows that the coefficient $d(d-1)/2$ cannot be increased, equality holds exactly for the measure-and-prepare channels with rank-one effects $\alpha_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$ and pure outputs $|\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k|$ whose overlaps are an affine image of those of the measurement directions, $|\langle\psi_j|\psi_k\rangle|^2 = P + (1-P)\,(d|\langle e_j|e_k\rangle|^2 - 1)/(d-1)$ for a common $P = \mathrm{Tr}\,\Phi(\mathbf{1}/d)^2$. These include the completely dephasing channel, the re-preparation channel of every rank-one POVM, a one-parameter family interpolating between dephasing and the constant channel, and non-unital non-projective examples already at $d = 2$. The qubit case reads $\|A\|_*^2+|c|^2\le1$ and extends to full rank a rank-two condition of Ruskai. The proof sharpens Ruskai's bound $\|A\|_*\le1$ by retaining the POVM completeness relation $\sum_k f_k=0$, which her argument discards; this recentres $A$ from a second moment into a cross-covariance, and is the entire content of the improvement.

papers.title: Non-Abelian sheaf quantum LDPC codes: good and magical
papers.authors: Zimu Li, Fuchuan Wei, Zhengyi Han, Zi-Wen Liu
papers.abstract: Non-Abelian quantum codes connect quantum error correction, phases of matter, and computational resources. In this work, we develop a general framework for constructing non-Abelian quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes by gauging sheaf codes via cup products and use it to establish code families with constant encoding rate and linear distance, simultaneously achieving optimal asymptotic scaling in both parameters. In particular, we characterize explicit logical representatives of the full gauged code space, and provide a fundamental treatment of non-Abelian code distance in the sense of Knill--Laflamme based on combining expansion with cleaning to establish protection against arbitrary errors. We further construct an almost-good family with entire code spaces exhibiting long-range magic. Moreover, we use linearly addressable cup product to directly generate linearly many encoded magic states from gauging measurements of Clifford operators. These results extend good qLDPC codes beyond the Pauli stabilizer setting, lay the foundation for pursuing the no low-energy trivial magic conjecture and shed light on non-Abelian quantum phases and orders beyond geometric locality.

papers.title: The Riemann theta function near soliton limit
papers.abstract: It has been known that (the square of) Jacobi elliptic function can be expressed by an infinite sum of single solitons of $\sech^2$ shape. In this paper, we show that there exists a similar structure for higher genus cases. It turns out that this is just a consequence of the quasi-periodicity of the Riemann $\theta$-function. More precisely, we show that the second derivative of $\log \theta$ with the \emph{real} Riemann $\theta$-function of genus $g$ near soliton limit can be well approximated by the \emph{sum} of \emph{real} and \emph{regular} $g$-soliton solutions of Hirota-type in $g$-dimensional real space $\R^g$. This leads to a tessellation of $\R^g$, whose tile is an oblique prism divided into $2^g$ sections by hyper-planes of dominant exponents in the theta function. We apply the results to study quasi-periodic solutions to the KdV and KP equations. We construct the quasi-periodic solutions using the Schottky group, which uniformizes the corresponding Riemann surfaces. We also discuss solitons on quasi-periodic background by pinching some of the homological cycles

papers.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
papers.authors: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu
papers.abstract:
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages. Fractional routing instead splits each message among source-destination paths and forwards its parts without combining different messages. For undirected networks carrying independent messages between multiple source-destination pairs, the multiple-unicast conjecture asserts that the two methods achieve the same combinations of message rates. We give a finite counterexample and use its linear structure to accelerate external-memory integer sorting, addressing the question of whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound posed by Aggarwal and Vitter in 1988.
  We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. In some parameter ranges, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean.

papers.title: Dimension-Optimal Dynamic Regret in Exp-Concave Online Learning
papers.authors: Yanyi Li, Wendao Wu, Haihan Zhang, Qinshi Wang, Chenheng Zhang, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
papers.abstract:
Tracking changing comparators is a central problem in online learning. For exp-concave losses, previous work established the $T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon $T$ and Euclidean path length $P_T$ for fixed dimension, while the optimal cost of dimension remained unresolved. We resolve this question by establishing a sharp $d^{1/3}$ curved dimension factor, improving the $d^{2/3}$ factor of recent switching and interval reductions [1, 2]. To achieve this improvement, we develop a proper, full-information learner on compact convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that adapts to the unknown path length and, under fixed dimension-independent diameter, gradient, and curvature parameters, guarantees
  $$\operatorname{Reg}_T(u_{1:T}) \le \widetilde{O}\left(d+\min\left\{d^{1/3}T^{1/3}P_T^{2/3},\sqrt{TP_T},T\right\}\right).$$
  A matching lower bound on a diameter-one Euclidean ball establishes the minimax frontier up to logarithmic factors when $T\gtrsim d^2$, including the transition from the curved rate to larger path budgets. The lower bound already holds for losses that depend on only one coordinate per round, isolating an unavoidable cost of learning across directions. Our upper bound follows from square-root Gaussian KL control of comparator movement and a cancellation argument that pays for history restarts. The curved learner maintains $O(\log^2 T)$ Gaussian states, uses one gradient per round, and runs in time near-linear in $T$ under a Mahalanobis-projection oracle.

papers.title: Separation of variables for coupled radiative perturbations of Kerr-Newman-de Sitter black holes
